readinessHtml:
INPATIENT ROTATION READINESS

For all inpatient rotations, it is highly recommended that you spend ½ day shadowing your predecessor before starting, as you are generally expected to hit the ground running on day one.

Shadowing is not an excused absence from your current rotation. Coordinate with your predecessor to shadow after hours or on a weekend to gain exposure to the service without interfering with your current rotation responsibilities.

Complete all required credentialing, EMR access, and facility access in advance of your start date.

Although PC/Chiefs are here to help and navigate, it is the incoming resident’s responsibility to ensure they are ready to begin the service. Confirm your readiness and any outstanding requirements with the program coordinator, chief residents, and service attending before the rotation begins, if needed.

Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation

St. Catherine’s West Rehabilitation Hospital

8850 NW 122nd St,

Hialeah, FL 33018

(305) 351-7181

Inpatient Acute Rehabilitation Service

Census: 10-14 patients each resident

Residents: 2 PGY-2 residents

MONDAY thru FRIDAY; cover 2 weekends each month (alternating weekends)

Attendings:

Colleen Neubert, MD (305) 797-4074
Miriam Feliz, MD (305) 915-6395

Things to do before rotating there:

1. Contact Ana Martinez, CPCS

Director of Medical Staff Services

Catholic Health Services

Office: 305-357-9795

Cell: 305-439-7491

Fax: 305-892-8627

Email: anamartinez@chsfla.com

Contact Ms. Ana Martinez two weeks prior to your rotation and complete all paperwork requested. She will provide you with EMR access after your paperwork is completed.

Spend ½ half of observation with the current resident prior to starting your rotation there to become familiar with documentation and procedure.

Receive a detailed sign out from the current resident on the patients that you will be taking over from him/her.

Rotation General Information:

1. Parking is available to residents in the spaces marked “reserved for physicians” in the front of the building.

2. Lunch is provided in the doctor’s work room to the residents.

3. Acute patient rooms are located on the 2nd floor. Your patients will be on the 2nd floor. The 3rd floor is for SNF and hospice patients. The PT/OT gym is located on the 1st floor. Speech therapy offices are also located on the 1st floor.

Rotation Responsibilities:

  1. Ask your Attending what time you should be there to meet and discuss patients. Arrive early enough to round on your patients and chart review prior to meeting your Attending to discuss the patients.

  2. Write all notes and enter all orders for your patients after discussing the patients with your Attending.

  3. Residents are responsible for new patient notes, progress notes, and discharge summaries.

  4. New patient notes must be completed and signed by your attending within 24 hours of the patient being admitted.

  5. Residents are required to participate in a team conference on M/T/W/Th (frequency of team conferences each week depend on census) and document the team conference summary as part of the patient’s progress note.

  6. Residents are expected to be present at every rapid response/code.

  7. Residents work M-F and every other weekend. Schedule is subject to change based on the request of your Attending physician. On weekend call, see your Attending’s full list on Saturday and write progress notes as well as new admissions assigned to any of the attendings on the weekend. On Sundays, you are only responsible to see the new admissions and write H&P for them.

  8. Be polite to all employees. You will be working closely with Therapists (PT/OT/SP), Nursing, and Case Managers.

QUICK REFERENCE

Role Name Contact
Attending Colleen Neubert, MD (305) 797-4074
Attending Miriam Feliz, MD (305) 915-6395
Director of Medical Staff Services Ana Martinez, CPCS Office (305) 357-9795; Cell (305) 439-7491; anamartinez@chsfla.com

Building

Floor What is there
1st PT/OT gym, speech therapy offices
2nd Acute patient rooms (your patients), offices
3rd SNF and hospice (not your responsibility)

Weekends (every other weekend)

Day What you do
Saturday See the attending's full list, write all progress notes, and admit new patients for any attending
Sunday New admissions only (write the H&P)

Study topics

  • IRF documentation (WellSky notes + ECS orders/labs)

  • Stroke, orthopedic and cardiopulmonary rehab

  • Discharge planning and disposition

Tips from residents

  • Your St. Catherine's (CHS) account also works at St. Anthony's, but it still has to be activated there.

  • Knock before entering rooms, do not interrupt patients during meals, and do not interview or examine patients outside their rooms.

Attendings

Colleen Neubert, MD

Miriam Feliz, MD

rotations.html:
Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation

Address:

4399 N Nob Hill Rd, Tamarac, FL 33321

Inpatient Acute Rehabilitation Service

Census: 90 bed hospital, expect to be constantly capped.

Residents: PGY-2 resident

MONDAY thru FRIDAY; cover 1-2 weekends each month (alternating weekends)

Contact:

Thiago Queiroz, DO

PM&R Attending

Cell: 205-835-4655

Rotation Coordinator Contact:

Reach out to: Dr. Queiroz and Mia Jones Mia.Jones@encompasshealth.com

Reach out at least 6 weeks in advance, follow up weekly until access and onboarding is initiated, this must be completed before your start date, and admin here is notoriously slow for getting your credentialing completed. .

General Information

  • Coordinate with Dr Queiroz about times of rounds every day.

  • Coordinate with NP Yaisel Barrero +1 (786) 236-4611 about distribution of patients.

Workflow

  • Arrive by: between 6:00 and 7:00 am, 2 hours prior to rounds

  • Aim for rounding by: between 8:00 and 9:00 am

  • Team conference time/expectations: every Wednesdays and Fridays at 9:00 am

  • Any special things to know for controlled substances/ placing orders/ admissions/ discharges: the system did not allow residents to do med recs, for controlled drugs, ask Dr Queiroz or Yaisel (NP) to place the orders.

  • Prechart any admits the night before. There is an AI tool (under the tab marked “Smart Tools”) that will generate an HPI for you.

    • AI tool is not always 100% accurate but is usually does a pretty good job and at least gives you a good starting spot for new admits

    • Look for any patients with a length of stay < 1.0 days

    • Will need to look through the previous facility’s documents to fill in the gap.

  • Lunch is provided in the cafeteria , no cost.

Rapid response expectations: not mandatory

Parking info: private parking outside the building . We can use anyone but the Physician’s spots.

QUICK REFERENCE

Role Name Contact
Attending (Medical Director) Thiago Queiroz, DO (205) 835-4655
Rotation Coordinator Mia Jones Mia.Jones@encompasshealth.com
NP (day-to-day operations) Yaisel Barrero (786) 236-4611

Study topics

  • High-volume IRF patient management

  • Encompass Health system protocols

  • Controlled-substance workflow in the hospital setting

Tips from residents

  • Credentialing is slow. Contact Dr. Queiroz and Mia Jones 6 weeks ahead and follow up weekly; silence does not mean progress.

  • Pre-chart new admits the night before. The AI tool under "Smart Tools" drafts an HPI; it is a starting point, not always accurate.

  • Residents cannot place controlled-substance or med-rec orders; ask Dr. Queiroz or Yaisel.

  • For patients with a length of stay under 1 day, review the prior facility's documents to fill in gaps.

Attendings

Thiago Queiroz, DO

rotations.html:
Before rotation, contact current residents on service to schedule ½ day observation and resident-to-resident patient sign out. PLEASE NOTE: this rotation is MERGED with the Waterford rotation.

Larkin Community Hospital (LCH) - South Miami Campus

7031 SW 62nd AVE, South Miami, FL 33143

http://www.larkinhospital.com

Inpatient PMR Consulting Service

Census: 10-15 patients per resident

Residents: PGY 2

Attendings: Jose Diaz, DO

MONDAY through FRIDAY

1 WEEK BEFORE:

  • COMPUTER ACCESS:

    • Make sure you have computer access at Larkin and at home (if you don't have access Carlos in IT can help):
      Email carlosp@larkinhospital.com, Phone +13052847711)

    • Larkin IT (305) 284-7554
      You may need a cookie: https://secure.larkinhospital.com/home/medhost

    • Make sure to have VPN Connect downloaded in order to have access at home (IT can help with this)

  • Go to Larkin main building (2nd Fl), try to login, get oriented and contact information from the previous resident.

  • PARKING: Get your parking pass during Orientation from HR and you will have access to free parking in the Resident Lot next to Miami Neuroscience Center

LARKIN SOUTH MIAMI CONSULT SERVICE - INSTRUCTIONS

  • Check for any TKA (Total Knee Arthroplasty) or THA (Total Hip Arthroplasty) cases (95% of orthopedic cases happen on Mondays and Wednesdays), also check for cases you think would benefit from rehabilitation

Steps:

  1. Go to Larkin, 2nd floor.

  2. Take the facesheet, scan it using the Notes app, and send it to the ISS front desk, ISS medical assistant, and ISS office manager.

  3. Log in to Medhost. Choose "My Group List" and click on the desired patient.

  4. On the facesheet, write the vital signs. Then, click on "Notes -> H&P" and write down the PMH (Past Medical History).

  5. Click on "Ancillary Notes" and look for PT (Physical Therapy) notes (usually written by Nelson). Write the PLOF (Prior Level of Function), for example: "Modified Independent with Rolling Walker. Lives with family in a single-level home, 1 step to enter."

  6. Next, write the CLOF (Current Level of Function), for example: "5 feet with RW, Max A."

  7. Look at the case manager notes to see D/C (Discharge) planning.

  8. Go say hi to patients, perform physical exams, etc.

  9. Write notes. See instructions below

  10. Text Dr. Diaz (`); he will call you around 4 pm to discuss cases.

HOW TO WRITE NOTES

  • We have to do our notes in HMS Medhost and copy them into WRS (just copy the whole HMS Medhost note into the HPI section on WRS, add your name under disposition, couple diagnoses, and billing code. The billing codes that we use in WRS system: New consults: Hospital, 99222 and Follow-ups: Hospital, 99232)

  • Ask Senior Resident for current WRS password

  • HMS Tips:

    • To access remotely, https://clinical.larkinhospital.com/

    • For notes you can use Quick Note template if you'd like, or the default HMS templates.

    • To find therapy progress notes, open the patient’s chart and choose:

    • Documents → Nursing. Then pick from the dropdown menu PTA, OT, ST, CM, etc... (most follow-up therapy will be under PTA but sometimes under PT, check both)

    • To find therapy initial evaluation, and MBS results open the patient’s chart and choose: Documents → Sum/Assessments

    • All notes/orders are cosigned to Dr. Diaz

    • Use this link that will guide you how to write notes in HMS Medhost https://www.loom.com/share/2bc098d95a6b4f6fbc0290980797e632

PATIENT LIST/ADMINISTRATIVE

  • Send patient list with facesheet PDFs for new patients. You can download the face sheets from medhost. At the top of the medhost clinical view screen, it is the "dashing sheet of paper" icon between the printer icon & computer screen icon. I usually send it from my home PC when I did quick chart review/census printing.

  • ***Send PATIENT LIST + FACESHEET to these contacts:

    • medassistant@integrativespineandsportsfl.com

    • frontdesk@integrativespineandsportsfl.com

    • officemanager@integrativespineandsportsfl.com

    • I sent this email from the Larkin PM&R gmail account (avoid using your personal account)

  • When doing notes, if you notice a patient name is misspelled please also send an email letting them know.

  • If two patients have similar names, please make it clear/stand out (i.e. put ****NAME ALERT**** )

  • Use this link to see instructions on how to use WRS https://www.loom.com/share/98fd0518019b43f686a23849ca53341a

Template

HPI/Subjective:

Interval History:

Patient seen and evaluated at bedside today. VSS, NAD, A&Ox4 . States that he feels well; pain level is a /10 at rest and /10 while ambulating; participating well in therapy and pain is not a limiting factor. today in therapy he walked 40 ft with a walker. She does complain of poor sleep due to pain Patient Denies N/V, Fever, Chills. Normal appetite and BMs. No new complaints at this time

PLOF: Independent
CLOF: Min A

ROS:
Constitutional: No fevers, weight loss, headache
Eyes: No change in vision or double vision
Ears, Nose, Mouth, Throat: Denies bleeding, masses, or changes in hearing
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, chest pressure or palpitations
Respiratory: Denies SOB, productive cough, trouble breathing
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation.
Genitourinary: Denies dysuria, hematuria, incontinence,
Musculoskeletal: (+) pain
Integumentary: Denies rash, easy bruisability, masses
Neurological: Denies dizziness, localized weakness or paresthesias
Psychiatric: Denies feelings of anxiety, depression
=========================================

T: HR: RR: BP:
GENERAL: The patient was alert and oriented 4 , in no acute distress.

SKIN: warm, dry, with good turgor, no sacral or heel ulcers present

HEENT: conjunctivae without inflammation, PERRLA, Oral hygiene and dentition was fair. Oral mucosa is moist

RESPIRATORY: Symmetrical expansion of the chest.

CARDIOVASCULAR: No significant edema was noted on both lower extremities.

ABDOMEN: Soft and depressible.

MUSCULOSKELETAL:

Full PROM in BUE and RLE

Decreased range of motion in LLE

NEUROLOGIC:

Followed commands appropriately

answered questions appropriately

Speech was grossly clear.

Muscle strength

BUE 5/5

_LE 5/5

_LE 3/5

CN II-XII grossly intact

DTR 2/4 throughout

Sensation to light touch grossly intact
Imaging:

Recommendations:
#Cardiopulmonary debility

- Due to patient’s current cardiopulmonary deconditioning status, recommend PT/OT only after

establishing hemodynamic stability to include O2 sat 90% without any forms of supplement O2, HR <120, or any symptoms such as exertional discomfort/pain in the chest upon physical exertion. Currently oxygenation well on room air, and is stable for appropriate PT/OT

#Gait abnormality/Balance dysfunction/Activities of daily living dysfunction

- Recommend physical therapy for functional assessment, therapeutic exercises, ADLs and IADLs and gait retraining. Occupational therapy for therapeutic exercises, ADLs and IADLs, transfer training, assisted device management if required and energy conservation techniques.

- Will follow along with therapists

- Monitor PO intake & BMs/I&Os

- WBAT

- Knee / Hip precautions in place

- Recommend discharging patient to home vs acute rehab, pending insurance approval

#Anemia
- Monitor CBC
- In bed therapy only if Hb <8 or symptomatic
- Out of bed therapy if Hb>8

#Pain

- Morphine 2mg PRN q3hr; OxyCodone 5mg PRN q6hr, Gabapentin 300mg HS

CM for discharge planning.

All medical management as per consult(s) and medicine team.

Thank you for allowing us to participate in this patient care. Pt seen and discussed with nursing, Therapy, CM and attending. The patient was seen and examined this morning by PM&R resident.

Signature Healthcare Center of Waterford

Subacute Care Rehab Consult Service

Before rotation, contact current residents on service to schedule ½ day observation and resident-to-resident patient sign out. PLEASE NOTE: this rotation is MERGED with the LCH South Consults rotation.

Address: 8333 W. Okeechobee Rd, Hialeah, FL 33016

Phone: (305) 556-9900

Website: http://shccenterofwaterford.com

Subacute Rehabilitation Consult Service

Census: 20 - 30 patients

Residents: 2 PGY-2 residents for 3 months

Attending: Dr. Stein

MONDAY through FRIDAY

Contact Numbers (Do not share)

Dr. Stein (516-578-7814)

Waterford instructions

  1. Contact Pedro Toro (don@waterford.care) and go in-person to Waterford to see him for EMR access (which is called PointClickCare).

  2. Next, email Dunia Castillo (bom@waterford.care), the business office manager at Waterford, to be added to her email list. She sends out emails regarding the Waterford census every day around 9-11 am (for weekend admissions, the email is sent out on Monday). These emails include information about new admissions, discharges, and transfers.

  3. See the example email from Dunia below. New admissions are listed at the top of the table, and you are responsible for patients with HMO insurance only. For example, in the table below, Raul Suarez is the only new patient for you to see that day.

  • Write all the patient notes in Word documents and email them to him (pjstein14@gmail.com), then call or text Dr. Stein (516-578-7814) to discuss the patients

  • Quick Summary of How to Use PointClickCare: Please see the video uploaded on drive called “Waterford EMR instruction video”

  • How to Do Patient Notes: Use the template provided below.

  • For physical therapy and OT notes, you need to ask the therapist to print them out for you because PointClickCare has limited access to those notes.

PARKING: Park in any unassigned spot. Park far away from the entrance, save the closer spots for visitors.

BUILDING: Ground/First Floor is Subacute; Second Floor is long term care; Third floor has Physical Therapy Main Gym for Team conference; Fourth Floor has Medical Records.
*ALL* of your patients will be on the first/ground floor. Admissions office near the ground floor lobby also has a red book which contains the functional status for the HMO patients.

SCHEDULE: **Someone must physically show up at Waterford Monday-Friday**

Monday: Contact Dr. Stein in the morning to determine the time of rounds. Morning round-independent

Tuesday: morning round -independent

Wednesday: morning round- independent

Thursday: morning rounds -independent

Friday: Virtual or in-person rounds (can vary, so be sure to reach out at the beginning of the week to determine modality of rounds, time and day of week)

GENERAL INFORMATION ABOUT WATERFORD ROTATION:

The patients are followed by a Primary doctor, usually Family Medicine and we are the Consultants. Do not overstep your boundaries. As a consultant, your job is to give recommendations. You are not managing these patients; your input is being requested by the managing physician. Keep in mind that this is a subacute rehab facility, not an acute rehab facility. Patients here are stable, but would not necessarily be able to tolerate 3 hours of rehab (as they would be subjected to in an acute rehab facility). The ground floor has both an OT and PT gym which is side by side. There is usually a Therapy Schedule for the day which is posted on the wall. It has the Patient's name, along with the Therapist assigned to them in a list format. The therapists are very approachable and are easy to talk to. At the nursing station, you will find the charts with the patient's name on the spine of the patient binder as well as the Primary Attending.

They are very keen on patients rights and elder abuse, so please make sure you knock on the door before you enter and treat everyone respectfully. Do not interrupt patients while they are eating. Do not interview or examine patients outside of their rooms. Do not be pushy with the nurses or primary attending physicians. You may have been previously trained in more fast-paced, high-volume facilities. This facility is more laid back, so don’t employ those habits in this environment.


Writing Notes

Use this template to write notes

PHYSICAL MEDICINE AND REHABILITATION CONSULTATION

REASON FOR CONSULT: Rehabilitation

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:

CLOF as of ___: (current level of function>> see Physical therapist and OT notes)

PLOF as of ___: (previous level of function>> see Physical therapist and OT notes)

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:

MEDICATIONS:

PAIN MEDICATION:

NUTRITION SUPPLEMENTS:

ALLERGIES:

Denies alcohol/tobacco/drug use.

FAMILY HISTORY:

Mother:

Sibling: 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:

History obtained from the patient and chart review.

General: Negative for chills, fatigue, fever, malaise, sleep disturbance

Psychological: Negative for anxiety, behavioral disorder, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, hostility, irritability, sleep disturbances

Ophthalmic: Negative for blurry vision, decreased vision, double vision, dry eyes, excessive tearing, eye pain, itchy eyes, and loss of vision

ENT: Negative for epistaxis, headaches, hearing change, nasal congestion, sinus pain, sneezing, sore throat, tinnitus, and vertigo.

Respiratory: Negative for cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, and wheezing

Cardiovascular: Negative for DOE, edema, irregular heartbeat, loss of consciousness, palpitations, rapid heart rate, and shortness of breath. 

Gastrointestinal: Negative for abdominal pain, appetite loss, change in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea, gas/bloating, heartburn, hematemesis, and N/V

Genito-Urinary: Negative for change in the urinary stream, hematuria, incontinence, pelvic pain, urinary frequency/urgency

Musculoskeletal: Negative for joint pain, joint stiffness, joint swelling, muscle pain, Positive for muscular weakness.

Neurological: Negative for behavioral changes, confusion, dizziness, headaches, memory loss, numbness/tingling, seizures, speech problems, tremors, and visual changes. Positive for impaired coordination/ balance, and weakness

Dermatological: Negative for dry skin, eczema, pruritus, rash and skin lesion changes, pressure injury, skin tear

VITALS

BP:

RESP:

PHYSICAL EXAM:

General appearance - Alert, well Appearing, and in no acute distress

Mental status – Alert and oriented X3. 

Eyes - pupils equal and reactive, extraocular eye movements intact

Chest - clear to auscultation, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi, symmetric air entry

Heart - normal rate, regular rhythm, normal S1, S2, no murmurs, rubs, clicks or gallops

Abdomen - soft, non-tender, non-distended, no masses or organomegaly. Normoactive BSx4

Neurological - Mental Status: The patient is alert, attentive, and oriented. Speech is clear.  CN: II through XII are grossly intact

   MMT:

      LUE: -3/5

      LLE:-3/5

      RUE: 3/5

      RLE: -3/5

Per PT/OT: RLE ROM = WFL; LLE ROM = WFL; RLE strength = impaired; LLE strength = impaired

Per PT/OT: RUE ROM = WFL; LUE ROM = Impaired; RUE strength = WFL; LUE strength = WFL

   Sensation: intact

   Coordination:

GOALS:

Prevent complications of immobilization

Increase functional activity tolerance, increase coordination, and increase independence with gait/mobility with appropriate AD as needed.

Increase independence in ambulation and safe transfers as appropriate.

Return to prior level of function at home.

-Medical management as per the primary Team

-Restorative PT/OT

-Pain management

-Pressure Injury prevention

PRECAUTION: 

PHYSICAL THERAPY:

Perform muscle strength evaluation and quantification.

Evaluate gait for lower extremity.

Evaluate muscle length and perform stretching exercises and soft tissue mobilization to enhance muscle elasticity.

Evaluate muscle hypotonicity or hypertonicity and provide exercises to normalize motor control.

Evaluate and train in sitting and standing balance, endurance and coordination, transfers, and mobility including wheelchair use, ambulation, and stair negotiation.

Assess total body posture and provide education and exercises to improve alignment.

Assess skin integrity and provide precautionary instructions for skin care.

Teach exercises to increase strength, endurance, and coordination for specific muscle groups or the entire body.

Restore and preserve joint range of motion through mobilization techniques and exercises.

Perform progressive gait training including instruction in negotiating barriers and obstacles.

Teach breathing exercises and incentive spirometry.

Assess equipment needs, including gait devices and wheelchair needs.

OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY:

Evaluate and train patient in self-care activities, transfer techniques

Aid in maintaining and improving joint range of motion, muscle strength, endurance, coordination, dexterity, particularly in the upper extremities.

Evaluate and train the patient to compensate for sensory, perceptual and cognitive deficits as they relate to function.

Patient/Family education.

Train patients or significant others in the maintenance of equipment.

GENERAL INFORMATION ABOUT WATERFORD ROTATION:

The patients are followed by a Primary doctor, usually Family Medicine and we are the Consultants. Do not overstep your boundaries. As a consultant, your job is to give recommendations. You are not managing these patients; your input is being requested by the managing physician. Keep in mind that this is a subacute rehab facility, not an acute rehab facility. Patients here are stable, but would not necessarily be able to tolerate 3 hours of rehab (as they would be subjected to in an acute rehab facility). The ground floor has both an OT and PT gym which is side by side. There is usually a Therapy Schedule for the day which is posted on the wall. It has the Patient's name, along with the Therapist assigned to them in a list format. The therapists are very approachable and are easy to talk to. At the nursing station, you will find the charts with the patient's name on the spine of the patient binder as well as the Primary Attending.

They are very keen on patients rights and elder abuse, so please make sure you knock on the door before you enter and treat everyone respectfully. Do not interrupt patients while they are eating. Do not interview or examine patients outside of their rooms. Do not be pushy with the nurses or primary attending physicians. You may have been previously trained in more fast-paced, high-volume facilities. This facility is more laid back, so don’t employ those habits in this environment.

  • Third floor: 3rd floor patient rooms, 3rd floor VR gym, 3rd floor dining room, 3rd floor nursing station

Long-Call

  • Residents must lay eyes on each new admission, and write at minimum 3 H&Ps as assigned by the admissions nurse (usually the first 3 admissions)

  • Gladys is the nurse for admissions. Her contact is (305) 297-3016. At 5-5:30PM you will receive a print out of projected admissions. This census will also be emailed to you if you have given your email to Yuri. The admission email will include the Pre-admission screening.

  • Must stay until 10 PM. Cannot leave premises when you are on call. It is your responsibility to be available to the nursing staff so you can answer their questions, evaluate patients they are concerned about and run rapid response &/or codes. In the event of an emergency, you must notify Dr. Vivaldi if for any reason you need to leave early.

EPIC:

For those who don’t want to log in to a computer to place orders, here are the instructions to get Epic on your phone. Whole process takes maybe 15 minutes

1. Download Haiku app

2. Call the EPIC help desk (888) 972-1199

4. Send the info to this email: smishaikurequests@selectmedical.com - They will send a link back to your email along with a PDF for user instructions.

5. Open the link on your phone, it will route to Haiku.

6. Login once Haiku opens and you’re golden 😊

PTO

  • You cannot take more than 5 days off in 3 months during this rotation (CME & Sick Days are not included)

Expectations

  • The night before, you should know who you are following and split up the census with your team with all projected admissions. New admissions should be divided accordingly (full hospital census will wax and wane, but you will carry between 12-14 patients on average).

  • Pre-round time varies per attending, generally arrive at 6:30-7AM.

  • New admissions have priority over established patients. Full H&P’s must be completed within 24 hours of new patient admission. This is VERY important. Check the time they arrived in the EMR.

  • PGY2 residents work with Dr. Mamsaang and Dr. Vivaldi. PGY3 residents work with Dr. Ortiz and Dr. Ramirez. If one service gets more than 3 admissions per resident (6 per team), the other residents will help out with the admit and then pass the patient off to the service that will follow the patient.

  • Your first physical exam must be your most thorough physical exam.

  • Check heels and sacrum on every patient, and document your findings. It is better to document “Minimal/moderate sacral erythema appreciated”, than to document, “No sacral skin breakdown.” Make sure the patient’s nurse is aware of your findings.

  • All progress notes should be completed by the end of your work day. Every progress note should include functional status, DVT prophylaxis, GI prophylaxis, and disposition.

  • Internal Medicine is the primary team, so PM&R residents do not write discharge summaries. A progress note is still required on the day of discharge.

  • You must be present at every rapid response. If a rapid response is announced, stop what you are doing immediately and go see the patient (unless you are in the middle of a procedure, of course.) PGY-2 residents are encouraged to run every rapid response.

  • If a patient is acutely sent to the hospital please attempt to get a hold of the IM and consulted physicians for recommendations and orders. Call your attending.

  • All residents are expected to remain present throughout the duration of team conference.

  • Contact Niurka Pedrera the administrative secretary and ask her which Attending is on call the weekend you are on call in a timely manner. Reach out to the on call Attending in a timely manner and ask them which time they start rounds, if you are expected to see new consults. Each Attending has their own style. Ask your seniors for tips.

  • You will be responsible for rounding on your patients, addressing any issues, and completing your notes. You will round with the attending on call that weekend.

  • Call your attending with any issues that are beyond your current level of expertise.

Academics

  • Grand Rounds: Grand rounds are held on Tuesday the 2nd & 4th week of the month in the 1st floor dining room at 10 am. When making a schedule, decide which resident will be presenting for each respective grand rounds and topic. Let Dr. Vivaldi know in advance which resident and topic they will be presenting. Presentations are typically 30 mins long.

  • Ask Dr. Vivaldi for the mini lecture with attendings schedule. It is your job to remind your Attendings of upcoming lectures, typically done during Friday at lunch time

  • Reach out OT/PT/SLP for lunchtime lectures on Tuesdays

GENERAL INFORMATION:

Dress professionally, (scrubs are acceptable, recommend wearing a white coat) unless otherwise instructed. Try to put as much energy as you can into this rotation.  The attendings are great doctors, and great people, and they are happy to have us onboard.  Get to know the therapists, as they will be able to provide you with insight into your patient's progress.  Remember that we are guests here, so act accordingly.  Treat the facility, therapists, nurses, and patients with respect.

WRITING NOTES:

Proper SOAP note writing is a skill that should have been acquired in medical school.  As a specialist, your progress notes should be more focused than when you were a medical student.  Avoid extraneous information, as it defeats the purpose of a progress note.  Just focus on what has happened since the last time you saw your patient.  Subjective section should include patient's current complaint (weakness, pain, difficulty breathing, etc.)  When describing pain, address onset, severity, quality, consistency, location, duration, and radiation.  A short review of systems, at the end of your subjective section, is always a good idea.  It is good practice to ask every patient about chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, eating, sleeping, and participation in therapy.

Start the objective section with vital signs (Tmax is useful if you are following a fever.)  Try to examine at least 7 areas on each exam, and include at least 3 findings in each area.

After the objective section, comment on the patient's functional status. Mobility, transfers, and ambulation are traditionally followed from physical therapy notes.  ADLs are traditionally followed from occupational therapy notes.  Speech therapy progress should be reported, if you are following a dysarthric or dysphagic patient.

If you are following labs or imaging studies, make sure you make a note of the results.

Assessment will address your patient's primary diagnosis, which is contributing to their gait and ADL dysfunction.  Your plan should be numbered in order of priority.  Number 1 will always be Gait and ADL dysfunction.  Here you should address how they are progressing, any barriers to progress, and whether or not any c es in their therapy regimen should be made.  Number 2 will be the primary diagnosis contributing to their gait and ADL dysfunction.  For example; Left TKA – Stable.  Decreased pain reported today.  Progressing well with therapy.  Continue pain medication.  Continue PT/OT.  Continue DVT PPx.  Follow-up with ortho on x/y/zzzz.  Monitor surgical site daily for any signs of infection.  Dressing changes daily, and as needed.  Remove staples on x/y/zzzz.  Et Cetera.  Number 3, and on, will be other diagnoses that you are following (but not necessarily managing).   It is perfectly fine to say ‘further management as per internal medicine’ for diabetes or hypertension, for example.  Close out your plan with DVT prophylaxis, GI prophylaxis, and disposition. Disposition is something that you will have to discuss with case managers.  Each day you should ask yourself: “Why is this patient here?”  “When will this patient be ready for discharge?”  “Will this patient be safe to return home, or will they require transfer to a SNF or LTAC?”

ROUNDING:

Reach out to attendings for specific rounding times as they may change day by day. Be ready to round by 7:30 AM with Dr. Ramirez. Dr. Vivaldi tends to round late morning or early afternoon. Dr. Ortiz rounds late afternoon. Dr. Mamsaang rounds at about 10am.

Finish chart reviewing and pre-rounding on patients before the attendings are ready to round with you.

TEAM CONFERENCE:

Dr. Ortiz Team Conference on Mondays and Wednesday 10:30 AM.

Dr. Vivaldi has Team Conference on Thursday at noon.

Dr. Ramirez has team conference on Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 AM

Dr. Mamsaang conference is Tuesdays and Friday at 12pm.

When sitting in team conference, be sure to pay attention to the following: For nursing, focus on continence, skin breakdown, and meal consumption.  For physical therapy, focus on mobility, transfers, and ambulation.  For occupational therapy, focus on upper body dressing, lower body dressing, and transfers.  For speech therapy, focus on communication, expression, aphasia, dysphagia and recommended diet.  For neuropsych, focus on objective measures of mental functioning, concentration, attention, memory, MMSE, and psychology. The question you should be asking yourself is “How is this patient progressing?”  “What are this patient’s barriers to progress?”  “What will this patient’s ultimate disposition be?”  Team conference is as much for the patient, as it is for the team.

rotations.html:
Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation

St. Anthony’s Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation

3487 NW 30th St.

Lauderdale Lakes, FL 33311

Inpatient Acute Rehabilitation Service

Census: 10-15 patients

Residents: 2 PGY-3/4 residents, who split the census (no PGY-2s)

MONDAY thru FRIDAY; cover 2 weekends each month (alternating weekends)

St. Anthony’s is the south building. The first floor is PT/OT and on the 2nd floor are patient rooms and offices. You will be seeing patients on the 2nd floor at St. Anthony’s only. (The 3rd and 4th floors are St. Joseph’s Assisted Living Facility. The north building is St. John’s Skilled Nursing Facility which residents are not responsible for, as we only have to see the St. Anthony’s patients instead).

http://www.catholichealthservices.org

Contact:

Thiago Queiroz, DO

Medical Director and Attending

Cell: 205-835-4655

Rotation Coordinator Contact:

Ana Martinez, CPCS

Director of Medical Staff Services

Cell: 305-439-7491

Email: amartinez@chsfla.com

General Information:

In general, outgoing residents will get in contact with HR and get the onboarding and credentialing going for incoming residents. It’s fairly straightforward since they only need to activate your account from St. Catherine’s. However if needed: get in touch with Ana Martinez at least 2 weeks prior to starting your rotation so you can fill out the required paperwork. As with all rotations make sure you have your updated PPD, yearly flu shot, current ACLS/BLS Certification. I recommend having your own personal copies of medical records so if a rotation site ever needs it you can send it quickly.

Make arrangements to spend an hour or two with prior residents for adequate sign out and rundown of workflow.

Responsibilities:

Dr. Queiroz (“Dr. Q”) is a former Larkin Chief resident who works with you to escalate your responsibilities and to be a fairly independent inpatient rehab resident by the end of the rotation. He will show you how team conferences are held at the beginning of the rotation, and by the end of the first month you should be able to lead a team conference on your own. Due to Dr. Q’s busy schedule as an inpatient physician in several other locations including Encompass, several MedSpas and another location in Orlando, his rounding time is quite variable but he still generally both residents to be present for most rounds and splitting the census (regardless of how low it can be at times), except for times when he notifies you in advance that he cannot physically round himself which may require you to coordinate with his APRN instead. Communicate with the previous resident regarding his most recent rounding schedule, but in general expect to arrive around 8 AM. You will receive a vital log every morning. Make sure all patients are stable then take new admissions and finally see your follow-ups. Admission notes must be completed within 24 hours of the patient being admitted so do these first. Progress notes are to be completed the day you see the patient. Notes are written on the CHS EMR WellSky, and labs are available every Tuesday on ECS. Orders are placed on ECS as well, similarly to St. Catherine’s. Team conferences are held at 10am on Tuesday for every patient, and at 10am on Thursday for every patient admitted since Tuesday of that week (patients admitted overnight onto Thursday will likely be postponed until the following Tuesday team rounds). On rare occasions, team conferences can be held earlier at 9AM, but this will be communicated and it is usually at Dr Q’s discretion. In general, the secretary and nursing staff would appreciate it if you verbally inform them of any STAT orders you place, any labs or consults you order, and any discharge medication reconciliation printouts which are performed for all patients (except those going to SNFs) upon discharge. The rotation is overall quite similar to St. Catherine’s West from the PGY-2 year.

Catholic Health Services is a great organization to rotate with and a core part of our residency program. Be respectful to others as you work as part of an interdisciplinary team that is critical to patient care.

Additional Info:

Dress: professional with scrubs and name badge

Parking: free, gate with guard will open automatically once you show guard your ID

Team conference days Tuesdays/Thursdays 10am

⚠ Confirm: the St. Anthony’s PGY-3/4 guide below reports a newer Monday/Friday 10 AM schedule. Check with Dr. Q.

You will mostly see stroke, ortho, cardiopulmonary and amputation rehab cases. Please familiarize yourself with treatment.

Recommended Readings: Braddom and Cuccurullo

Attending (Medical Director) Thiago Queiroz, DO ("Dr. Q") (205) 835-4655
Rotation Coordinator Ana Martinez, CPCS amartinez@chsfla.com; (305) 439-7491
Weekend NP (occasional) Mariela Rios (786) 319-6537
Nursing Supervisor Josee ask at the nursing station

Weekends (alternating)

Day What you do
Saturday See all patients and new admissions and write notes on all of them
Sunday New admissions only (write the H&P)

Study topics

  • Advanced spasticity management (oral agents, botulinum toxin)

  • Complex SCI and TBI rehab

  • Leading interdisciplinary team conference

  • Managing medically complex rehab patients independently

ST. ANTHONY'S PGY-3/4 GUIDE: A DAY IN THE LIFE

Written by residents for residents.

Census: 22 rooms (201–222); some rooms have more than one bed. The 2 PGY-3/4 residents split the census.

Hours: Dr. Q wants a resident in the hospital from 8 AM to 12 PM every day. Both residents do not need to be there the whole time; you can split shifts (for example 8–10 and 10–12). Be responsible and plan it with your co-resident.

Rounding: Dr. Q comes at different times, sometimes 6 AM on his own (he does not expect you then). For new patients he usually comes between 8 and 12 and asks the resident to present.

Team conference: 10 AM, usually in the big conference room (sometimes the small one; ask the nurses). If you are on the 10–12 shift, come early on team days and be prepared.

⚠ Confirm: this guide reports team conference on Monday and Friday (plus Thursday if needed for Monday/Tuesday-night admits); the section above says Tuesday/Thursday. Check with Dr. Q or Kristina (PPS coordinator) and update both.

  • Smaller overall patient load.

  • Dr. Q gives you much more independence to order what you think is best (within reason and what is available). You do not need to run everything by him, as long as you keep him informed.

  • No one double-checks your orders the way Drs. Feliz and Neubert did, so be diligent. The nurses will often catch duplicate or wrong-chart orders.

  • Place the order in ECS and write a prescription on the prescription pad (in the bin behind the nursing station), usually 30 tablets, and tell the nurses.

  • Write the script at least the day before discharge so Dr. Q can sign it in the morning. For weekend discharges, have it written by Friday.

  1. Go to "View/Edit Current Orders" and click every medication the patient is going home on (the text turns red). Double-check the selection.

General Information:

In general, outgoing residents will get in contact with HR and get the onboarding and credentialing going for incoming residents. However if needed: get in touch with Ana Martinez at least 2 weeks prior to starting your rotation so you can fill out the required paperwork. I recommend having your own personal copies of medical records so if a rotation site ever needs it you can send it quickly.

Make arrangements to spend an hour or two with prior residents for adequate sign out and rundown of workflow.

Responsibilities:

Dr. Queiroz (“Dr. Q”) is a former Larkin Chief resident who works with you to escalate your responsibilities and to be a fairly independent inpatient rehab resident by the end of the rotation. He will show you how team conferences are held at the beginning of the rotation, and by the end of the first month you should be able to lead a team conference on your own. Due to Dr. Q’s busy schedule as an inpatient physician in several other locations including Encompass, several MedSpas and another location in Orlando, his rounding time is quite variable but he still generally both residents to be present for most rounds and splitting the census (regardless of how low it can be at times), except for times when he notifies you in advance that he cannot physically round himself which may require you to coordinate with his APRN instead. Communicate with the previous resident regarding his most recent rounding schedule, but in general expect to arrive around 8 AM. You will receive a vital log every morning. Make sure all patients are stable then take new admissions and finally see your follow-ups. Admission notes must be completed within 24 hours of the patient being admitted so do these first. Progress notes are to be completed the day you see the patient. Notes are written on the CHS EMR WellSky, and labs are available every Tuesday on ECS. Orders are placed on ECS as well, similarly to St. Catherine’s. Team conferences are held at 10am on Tuesday for every patient, and at 10am on Thursday for every patient admitted since Tuesday of that week (patients admitted overnight onto Thursday will likely be postponed until the following Tuesday team rounds). The rotation is overall quite similar to St. Catherine’s West from the PGY-2 year.

Catholic Health Services is a great organization to rotate with and a core part of our residency program. Be respectful to others as you work as part of an interdisciplinary team that is critical to patient care.

Dress: Scrubs and VA PIV card.

Scheduling: M-F (some days are heavier EMG than others) time spent with clinic and EMG/NCS

Responsibilities:

  • Clinic daily (US guided procedures, PRP, Botox/Spasticity, TBI, P&O, Wheelchair, Prolotherapy, Spinal procedures) and EMG’s during mornings (+ a few afternoons). Multiple procedures possible. Maintain procedure log.  If appropriate, ask your attending prior to performing OMT.  Also, there are many enthusiastic attendings on the WPB VA PM&R team that are interested in lecturing.  They will be contributing to LCH PM&R didactics.

  • Become well acquainted with Neurodiagnostic equipment, tools, understanding of anatomy, and how to use EDX in practice.

  • PGY 4 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day with the exception of didactic sessions (typically held Monday and the third Thursday of the month from 2-6p).

  • PGY 3 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day 1-2 days a week. They both attend once per week at minimum for EMGs.

Attendance:

  • At the VA, the resident’s attendance will be kept track of by PGY4 seniors and Dr Reid at the end of each rotation month. This will be emailed to Kendra Morris and tracked. A copy of all PTO and coverage forms should be printed and given to Dr. Reid for her records. All attendings and co-residents should be notified in advance for PTO.

  • PTO: To be signed by Dr. Reid within the first week of the rotation - negotiable during the rotation.

  • Larkin Community Hospital (LCH) will monitor attendance by tracking PTO forms (copy of each is available from the program coordinator). A calendar or list will also be kept by the PMR chief resident.

  • In the EMG room, there is a maximum capacity for 3 PMR residents. This is generally, 2 PGY4 residents from LCH and 1 PMR resident from Broward Health North (BHN). If there are 3 PGY4 residents from LCH scheduled at the same time, they will alternate fairly to the outpatient clinic to maintain 3 residents total in the EMG room.

  • When a LCH PGY-3 resident joins the EMG rotation on Wednesdays and Thursdays, one-two of the LCH PGY-4 residents or BHN resident currently in EMG will be expected to voluntarily transition to the outpatient clinic to maintain appropriate staffing. The resident transitioning to the outpatient clinic should alternate fairly between LCH and BHN.

  • Fluoroscopy Suite Restriction: Please note that residents will not be permitted to rotate through the fluoroscopy suite during the upcoming academic year until further notice.

  • PGY 3 residents may be asked to cover shifts, and a PTO form will be required with their signature, on the days that do not interfere with other parts of their rotation (coverage should not interfere with Dr. Fishman/Dr. Romero (Tues) or Dr. Diaz (Fri when there are EMGs)).

  • Of the 4 residents on EMG/ISS and the VA there should be no overlapping PTO unless there are extenuating circumstances.

Didactic Attendance: Virtual attendance is required.

West Palm VA EMG Article presentation: Dr. Reid will assign an article to present and work with all residents to schedule a time during lunch (usually Tuesdays and Fridays).

Recommended Reading:

Delisa Frontera 3rd EMG Chapter 15 (about 42 pages) *Table on page 355

Liveson, Jay. Peripheral Neurology: Case Studies. Third Edition. New York: Oxford University Press Inc., 2000. Print.

Preston DC, Shapiro BE.  Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders, 2nd Edition.  Boston: Butterworth-Heineman, 2005. Print.

Visco, Christopher J, Gary P Chimes, and James P McLean. Mclean Course In Electrodiagnostic Medicine. New York: Demos Medical, 2010.

Weiss, Lyn D, J K. Silver, and Jay Weiss. Easy Emg: A Guide to Performing Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography. Edinburgh: Butterworth-Heinemann, 2004. Paperback.

Suggested Reading from American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine (AANEM):  http://www.aanem.org/Education/Resources/References/Suggested-Reading.aspx

WPB VA PGY-4 GUIDE (SEPT 2026)

Written by a PGY-4 who just completed the rotation.

Getting access set up

PIV card and Windows: Log in to VA computers with your PIV card and PIN. If Windows says your account is disabled, call IT; they may ask someone with an active VA email (such as another resident) to verify you with a code.

Office 365 and CPRS: In YourIT, request Microsoft Office 365 (Outlook and Teams); access usually works by your next login. For CPRS, open VA Shortcuts and select CPRSChart WPB (make a desktop shortcut).

Patient Check-In lists: In Edge go to VA Bookmarks → VHA → Patient Check In, Clinical Staff View. Make an EMG list (all EMG attendings' clinics) and a Pain/MSK/PRP list, and keep the EMG list open on the second monitor. If a patient looks like a no-show, call for them before assuming they are absent.

⚠ Confirm: as of 9/29/26 residents lost access to Patient Check-In after a security change (IT: access now needs security keys through EPAS). Ask Kendra Morris or Dr. García-Negrón.

Creating your CPRS electronic signature code

Your signature code is separate from your PIV PIN and is created in VistA. Set it up early and keep it private (never put it in a template).

  1. Open VistA (Gold Star or VA Shortcuts). At the Main Menu enter TB (Toolbox), then ELE.

  2. Check your initials, signature block name and title (all in CAPS) and your VA office phone (not your cell). If REPLACE appears when editing your title, enter "...", press Enter, and retype the title in CAPS at WITH.

  3. Create the code: 6–20 letters or numbers, all uppercase, no Ctrl characters. Typing does not show on screen. Re-enter it to verify, then press Enter until you leave the Toolbox.

  4. If you skip the prompt or mistype the confirmation, go back to the Main Menu and repeat.

CPRS clinic assignments (search "WPB Rehab EMG")

Clinic Attending
I Dr. Fitzig
II Dr. Reddy
III Dr. Reid-Artist
IV Dr. García-Negrón
V Dr. Cuevas
VI Dr. Garcia
X Dr. Woo (former)

Expectations and presentations

  • All scheduled EMG clinics are mandatory: take part in the studies and finish the documentation.

  • The two PGY-4s and the Broward EMG resident alternate presentations on Tuesdays and Fridays, about 12:15–12:50 PM. Keep Dr. Reid-Artist informed.

  • To schedule: Outlook → Calendar on the VA desktop → create the meeting → add a Teams link → invite all attendings. Email the slides to your VA email beforehand (Google Drive/Slides is unreliable on VA computers).

The EMG workflow

Start the machine: Turn on the monitor and the Cadwell (switch on the back left). Open Sierra and log in with username admin and password admin (press Enter if another prompt appears). For a new patient enter first name, last name and last four SSN digits as the ID. Click Start and pick a template (Bruno Upper Extremity, Bruno Lower Extremity, Cuevas).

Open the patient in CPRS: Clinic → search WPB Rehab EMG → choose the numbered clinic → choose the patient. "Save Clinic for Current Day" saves repeating the search. Useful tabs: Cover Sheet (PMH, meds, BMI); Reports → Local Imaging; Labs (A1c etc.); Consults (the EMG referral).

Review the consult: Open the most recent EMG referral; note the referring provider, reason, history and any attending recommendations. Decide which nerves to test before you start (attendings have different preferences).

Save note templates: Open a chart, create a temporary note, click Templates (lower left) → right-click → Create/Edit Template → name it, paste the text, Apply. Discard the temporary note. Shared templates: Shared Template → Physical Medicine → PM&R Physicians → EDx. Update the resident names in the signature section.

Start the note from the consult: Action → Consult Results → Complete/Update Results, so the note stays linked to the consult; pick the EMG note and the attending as co-signer. If Consult Results is grayed out, ask IT for: PAIN PROCEDURE OUTPATIENT; PHYSICAL MED & REHAB (EMG/NCS) OUTPATIENT; REHAB MD OUTPATIENT (the same permissions as your co-resident).

Write the note: Copy the referring provider and exact consult reason from the EMG order (use Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V). Update age, sex, handedness and a focused history (onset and progression, diabetes, thyroid disease, alcohol, prior treatment, prior EMG/NCS). Find prior VA study numbers for comparison. Use "Save Without Signature" for unfinished notes.

Results: Line up decimal points under the correct L/R columns. Wording: latency "prolonged", amplitude "low", conduction velocity "slow/slowed"; match singular/plural to the number of nerves or muscles. Interpret each nerve as you finish it and mark it with an asterisk.

Sign: Choose the correct attending as co-signer. Do not make yourself the primary provider (answer No or change it to the attending). Sign with your CPRS signature code.

Cadwell / Sierra tips

Control What it does
Scroll wheel Stimulus intensity
1 Distance entry (press 1, scroll to the cm value, press Store or 1)
2 Next nerve (arrange nerves in the order you will do them)
3 Averaging on/off (also the X-with-bar button on the Cadwell)
+/− Polarity (green probe light shows direction; for routine NCS point current toward the recording electrodes; F-waves and H-reflexes are exceptions)
Store Saves the selected waveform (it turns from white to purple)

  • Switching nerves resets intensity and polarity. Wipe gel off the probe between patients (alcohol swabs work well).

  • Drag nerves to reorder the list; moving finished nerves to the top keeps them separate.

  • To delete saved waveforms, Ctrl-click the purple ones, press Delete and confirm, then press F5 (Sort Traces) to reorder by latency.

  • To reuse an earlier trace, click the multiple-waveform icon next to the star (upper right), select one trace (it turns yellow) and replace. Selecting two averages them into a blue trace.

  • Add a nerve: right-click the nerve list → Insert (or the star icon). Add a study: star icon → Studies. If laterality is wrong, right-click the nerve and swap sides; no need to repeat the study.

  • End of day: turn off the Cadwell (back left switch) and the monitor. Do not shut down the computer.

  • Clinic daily (US guided procedures, PRP, Botox/Spasticity, TBI, P&O, Wheelchair, Prolotherapy, Spinal procedures) and EMG’s during mornings (+ a few afternoons). Multiple procedures possible. Maintain procedure log.  If appropriate, ask your attending prior to performing OMT.  Also, there are many enthusiastic attendings on the WPB VA PM&R team that are interested in lecturing.  They will be contributing to LCH PM&R didactics.

  • Become well acquainted with Neurodiagnostic equipment, tools, understanding of anatomy, and how to use EDX in practice.

  • PGY 4 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day with the exception of didactic sessions (typically held Monday and the third Thursday of the month from 2-6p).

  • PGY 3 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day 1-2 days a week. They both attend once per week at minimum for EMGs.

Attendance:

  • At the VA, the resident’s attendance will be kept track of by PGY4 seniors and Dr Reid at the end of each rotation month. This will be emailed to Kendra Morris and tracked. A copy of all PTO and coverage forms should be printed and given to Dr. Reid for her records. All attendings and co-residents should be notified in advance for PTO.

  • PTO: To be signed by Dr. Reid within the first week of the rotation - negotiable during the rotation.

  • Larkin Community Hospital (LCH) will monitor attendance by tracking PTO forms (copy of each is available from the program coordinator). A calendar or list will also be kept by the PMR chief resident.

  • In the EMG room, there is a maximum capacity for 3 PMR residents. This is generally, 2 PGY4 residents from LCH and 1 PMR resident from Broward Health North (BHN). If there are 3 PGY4 residents from LCH scheduled at the same time, they will alternate fairly to the outpatient clinic to maintain 3 residents total in the EMG room.

  • When a LCH PGY-3 resident joins the EMG rotation on Wednesdays and Thursdays, one-two of the LCH PGY-4 residents or BHN resident currently in EMG will be expected to voluntarily transition to the outpatient clinic to maintain appropriate staffing. The resident transitioning to the outpatient clinic should alternate fairly between LCH and BHN.

  • Fluoroscopy Suite Restriction: Please note that residents will not be permitted to rotate through the fluoroscopy suite during the upcoming academic year until further notice.

  • PGY 3 residents may be asked to cover shifts, and a PTO form will be required with their signature, on the days that do not interfere with other parts of their rotation (coverage should not interfere with Dr. Fishman/Dr. Romero (Tues) or Dr. Diaz (Fri when there are EMGs)).

  • Of the 4 residents on EMG/ISS and the VA there should be no overlapping PTO unless there are extenuating circumstances.

Didactic Attendance: Virtual attendance is required.

Written by a PGY-4 who just completed the rotation.

Getting access set up

PIV card and Windows: Log in to VA computers with your PIV card and PIN. If Windows says your account is disabled, call IT; they may ask someone with an active VA email (such as another resident) to verify you with a code.

Office 365 and CPRS: In YourIT, request Microsoft Office 365 (Outlook and Teams); access usually works by your next login. For CPRS, open VA Shortcuts and select CPRSChart WPB (make a desktop shortcut).

Patient Check-In lists: In Edge go to VA Bookmarks → VHA → Patient Check In, Clinical Staff View. Make an EMG list (all EMG attendings' clinics) and a Pain/MSK/PRP list, and keep the EMG list open on the second monitor. If a patient looks like a no-show, call for them before assuming they are absent.

⚠ Confirm: as of 9/29/26 residents lost access to Patient Check-In after a security change (IT: access now needs security keys through EPAS). Ask Kendra Morris or Dr. García-Negrón.

Creating your CPRS electronic signature code

Your signature code is separate from your PIV PIN and is created in VistA. Set it up early and keep it private (never put it in a template).

  1. Open VistA (Gold Star or VA Shortcuts). At the Main Menu enter TB (Toolbox), then ELE.

  2. Check your initials, signature block name and title (all in CAPS) and your VA office phone (not your cell). If REPLACE appears when editing your title, enter "...", press Enter, and retype the title in CAPS at WITH.

  3. Create the code: 6–20 letters or numbers, all uppercase, no Ctrl characters. Typing does not show on screen. Re-enter it to verify, then press Enter until you leave the Toolbox.

  4. If you skip the prompt or mistype the confirmation, go back to the Main Menu and repeat.

Expectations and presentations

  • All scheduled EMG clinics are mandatory: take part in the studies and finish the documentation.

  • The two PGY-4s and the Broward EMG resident alternate presentations on Tuesdays and Fridays, about 12:15–12:50 PM. Keep Dr. Reid-Artist informed.

  • To schedule: Outlook → Calendar on the VA desktop → create the meeting → add a Teams link → invite all attendings. Email the slides to your VA email beforehand (Google Drive/Slides is unreliable on VA computers).

The EMG workflow

Start the machine: Turn on the monitor and the Cadwell (switch on the back left). Open Sierra and log in with username admin and password admin (press Enter if another prompt appears). For a new patient enter first name, last name and last four SSN digits as the ID. Click Start and pick a template (Bruno Upper Extremity, Bruno Lower Extremity, Cuevas).

Open the patient in CPRS: Clinic → search WPB Rehab EMG → choose the numbered clinic → choose the patient. "Save Clinic for Current Day" saves repeating the search. Useful tabs: Cover Sheet (PMH, meds, BMI); Reports → Local Imaging; Labs (A1c etc.); Consults (the EMG referral).

Review the consult: Open the most recent EMG referral; note the referring provider, reason, history and any attending recommendations. Decide which nerves to test before you start (attendings have different preferences).

Save note templates: Open a chart, create a temporary note, click Templates (lower left) → right-click → Create/Edit Template → name it, paste the text, Apply. Discard the temporary note. Shared templates: Shared Template → Physical Medicine → PM&R Physicians → EDx. Update the resident names in the signature section.

Start the note from the consult: Action → Consult Results → Complete/Update Results, so the note stays linked to the consult; pick the EMG note and the attending as co-signer. If Consult Results is grayed out, ask IT for: PAIN PROCEDURE OUTPATIENT; PHYSICAL MED & REHAB (EMG/NCS) OUTPATIENT; REHAB MD OUTPATIENT (the same permissions as your co-resident).

Write the note: Copy the referring provider and exact consult reason from the EMG order (use Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V). Update age, sex, handedness and a focused history (onset and progression, diabetes, thyroid disease, alcohol, prior treatment, prior EMG/NCS). Find prior VA study numbers for comparison. Use "Save Without Signature" for unfinished notes.

Results: Line up decimal points under the correct L/R columns. Wording: latency "prolonged", amplitude "low", conduction velocity "slow/slowed"; match singular/plural to the number of nerves or muscles. Interpret each nerve as you finish it and mark it with an asterisk.

Sign: Choose the correct attending as co-signer. Do not make yourself the primary provider (answer No or change it to the attending). Sign with your CPRS signature code.

Cadwell / Sierra tips

Control What it does
Scroll wheel Stimulus intensity
1 Distance entry (press 1, scroll to the cm value, press Store or 1)
2 Next nerve (arrange nerves in the order you will do them)
3 Averaging on/off (also the X-with-bar button on the Cadwell)
+/− Polarity (green probe light shows direction; for routine NCS point current toward the recording electrodes; F-waves and H-reflexes are exceptions)
Store Saves the selected waveform (it turns from white to purple)

  • Switching nerves resets intensity and polarity. Wipe gel off the probe between patients (alcohol swabs work well).

  • Drag nerves to reorder the list; moving finished nerves to the top keeps them separate.

  • To delete saved waveforms, Ctrl-click the purple ones, press Delete and confirm, then press F5 (Sort Traces) to reorder by latency.

  • To reuse an earlier trace, click the multiple-waveform icon next to the star (upper right), select one trace (it turns yellow) and replace. Selecting two averages them into a blue trace.

  • Add a nerve: right-click the nerve list → Insert (or the star icon). Add a study: star icon → Studies. If laterality is wrong, right-click the nerve and swap sides; no need to repeat the study.

  • End of day: turn off the Cadwell (back left switch) and the monitor. Do not shut down the computer.

Integrative Spine & Sports (ISS)

Attending: Dr. Jose Diaz (PM&R Program Director)

Office Hours: Monday – Friday, Begin at 8-9 AM. Weekend: Residents on rotation will split Saturday shifts (office is open half day Saturday). Make your weekend work schedule with senior residents on the service.

Location:

3308 NE 34th St, Ft. Lauderdale, 33308

Office Phone: (954)-564-3200 Fax: (954)-653-9188

Dress Code: Scrubs

Need: Laptop, Reflex Hammer

EMR System: (WRS) http://www.waitingroomsolutions.com/

Rotation Responsibilities and Protocols

By following these procedures, you ensure a smooth and efficient start to your day, helping to maintain a high standard of patient care and team communication.

  1. Morning Commute:

    • Leave Early: Be sure to leave early, as traffic on Oakland Avenue can be unpredictable and often hectic. Allow extra time in the morning to ensure timely arrival at the office.

  2. Upon Arrival:

    • Log-in Procedure: Once you arrive, log in to the WRS (Workplace Reporting System).

    • Patient Status: Patient names displayed in blue indicate that they have arrived and are waiting in a room to be seen.

    • Room Assignment: Speak with the senior resident to confirm the room number of the waiting patients.

  3. Uniform Afternoon Stay: All residents are required to remain on duty until the afternoon. Early departures are not permitted unless explicitly approved by the attending physician.

  4. Dismissal Protocol: Senior residents are not authorized to dismiss medical students or junior residents. Only attending physicians have the authority to grant dismissal at the end of the workday.

  5. Medical Student Responsibilities:

    • Non-Procedural Role: Medical students are not licensed to perform procedures independently. Their primary responsibilities include taking notes, conducting patient intakes and interviews, and observing procedures performed by residents.

    • Liability Awareness: Given that medical students are not insured to perform procedures, it is critical to adhere to this protocol to avoid liability issues (NO NEEDLE STICKS!!!).

    • Inpatient rotation: if rotators are requesting inpatient experience they will require a level 2 background check with fingerprinting to be initiated at least 2 weeks prior to the hospital start date, and informing the attending (either Dr. Neubert or Dr. Vivaldi) of the medical student’s available dates.

    • Medical students are here to learn and as such, having them complete notes should not supersede their educational needs. As a general rule, each resident on service should be writing more notes than any medical student rotating in the clinic each day. This is in addition to and not including patient visits that the resident may supervise the medical student for. Residents are still responsible for seeing their own patients and writing their own notes. Reports of residents not pulling their weight in the clinic will be handled as a lack of professionalism.

  6. Educational Opportunities:

    • Informal Presentations: Senior residents should allocate time for junior residents and medical students to conduct mini informal presentations 2-3 times per week.

By adhering to these guidelines, we ensure the safety of our patients, the legal compliance of our practices, and the educational enrichment of our medical team.

Established Patients: You will (for most patients) begin each patient with Electric Stimulation machines and heating pads. Have a senior resident show you how to use the E-stim if you are unfamiliar. After that, you go in, and talk to patients about current HPI, work on them with osteopathic manipulation (use common sense with elderly or injured), find out how the medications (if any) are controlling their pain levels, constipation, side effects, etc. Present to Dr. Diaz when he’s available, see the patient with him after you present. Some will request routine trigger point injections or joint injections. If you are unfamiliar, this is a great rotation to practice, you will do them daily. You also will be learning and using acupuncture techniques, ultrasound, and fluoroscopy occasionally. Become familiar with how to use this equipment early in your rotation so you won’t waste time learning it when you get to use it. When you are done seeing the patient, you will be responsible for cleaning your patient room (that involves taking the bed sheets each time, putting them in the laundry room, and replacing each room with clean sheets. Unplug any cords to any devices that patients could potentially trip over).

New Patients: With new patients, perform a complete H&P, formulate a list of differential diagnosis/workup/treatment plan in your head, and then present to Dr. Diaz. He will guide you through the encounter, and you will learn a lot about patient care with new patients in this office.

Notes: You will write your notes immediately after your patient encounter. If you do not finish your note before the next patient arrives, be sure you write down any procedures you performed, or any specialized equipment used (such as Ultrasound) as this will be important when you code for billing at the end of the note. *Please be aware that if a patient has Medicare B insurance, then you will NOT list certain procedures (such as E-stim, modalities, etc..) because Medicare does not reimburse for it, so you do not want to bill for it.

It is our responsibility to code and “marry” diagnosis with code.

99214: EVERY established patient

99204: EVERY new patient

G0283: E-stim

9892..: for OMT depending on the # of body regions, aim for 7-8 or 9-10

Body regions referred to are: head region; cervical region; thoracic region; lumbar region; sacral region; pelvic region; lower extremities, upper extremities; rib cage region; abdomen and viscera region.

Injections: Use tabs to code for trigger point or joint injection, also code for what medication is used under the “medication” tab.

98711 or 98713: Acupuncture +/- stim

*INCOMPLETE NOTES or MISSING CODING MAY RESULT IN FAILURE OF ROTATION*

Tips:

  1. Office Procedures: On your first day, make sure to have a thorough orientation with the office manager to understand how things operate. This will help you integrate into the workflow smoothly.

  2. Respect Dr. Diaz's Time: Dr. Diaz is busy, so try to solve minor issues or questions yourself before bringing them to him. This shows respect for his time and demonstrates your independence in problem-solving.

  3. Self-Sufficiency: Bring snacks and drinks to sustain yourself during busy periods. Finding a moment to snack can help keep your energy levels up until you can take a proper break.

  4. Ultrasound Machine Usage: Follow the protocol for using the ultrasound machine diligently. Always keep it plugged in during use and storage to avoid data loss. Familiarize yourself with its functions early on so you're prepared to use it efficiently.

  5. Cell Phone Usage: Avoid using your cell phone for personal matters during work hours. Save it for lunch breaks to maintain professionalism and focus on your duties.

  6. Punctuality: Notify the office if you're going to be late, and inform your co-residents promptly. Punctuality is crucial in maintaining the efficiency of the workplace.

  7. Patient Safety: Always review a patient's medical history before any procedures, especially injections. This is crucial for handling situations like accidental needle sticks with patients who have infectious conditions.

  8. Proper Disposal and Protection: Dispose of needles in sharps containers and wear gloves during procedures to ensure safety. Additionally, wear a lead apron in the fluoroscopy lounge to minimize radiation exposure.

Student rotator templates:

New rotator email

Hello xxxx, Happy to have you on board for this month!

Please arrive by 8:15AM on [Date] to 3308 NE 34th St, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33308 (Integrative Spine and Sports).

Park on the side of the lot closer to the street (the post office does not appreciate taking easy access parking from older customers). The entire lot is free.

Attire is scrubs without white coat. Bring your student ID badge for identification.

Please bring a laptop and charger, [Seniors on rotation] will orient you that morning for workflow.

Prior to arrive, please a review a neuromuscular physical exam (strength grading, deep tendon reflexes, dermatomes, myotomes, how to distinguish axillary vs radicular back pain), MSK exam (hips, shoulders, knees, elbows, back), identification and management of common peripheral nerve injuries and multimodal pain medication regimens as these are common sources of discussion with the program director for patient recommendations. You will be asked to present on a rehab or pain topic of your choosing once per week.

Please let us know at least 2 weeks in advance if you wish to include inpatient acute rehab exposure for this rotation as it requires a level 2 background check with fingerprinting.

Expectations of rotators: You will be documenting patient encounters and learning how to bill for encounters and procedures as well. Due

We also have didactics each Monday at 2pm, If you have any questions for clarification, please direct these to [senior on rotation]

Attending (Program Director) Jose Diaz, DO drjosejuandiaz@gmail.com
Office – medical assistant — medassistant@integrativespineandsportsfl.com
Office – front desk — frontdesk@integrativespineandsportsfl.com
Office – manager — officemanager@integrativespineandsportsfl.com

Study topics

  • MSK physical exam

  • Reading MRI and X-ray for spine and joint pathology

  • Outpatient procedures: joint, bursa and trigger point injections; ultrasound-guided procedures

  • Clinical management algorithms for common diagnoses

Tips from residents

  • Know your anatomy cold; Dr. Diaz quizzes on ultrasound-guided injection landmarks.

  • Do not over-rely on imaging; the exam drives decisions.

  • Always consent and document procedures properly.

  8. Proper Disposal and Protection: Dispose of needles in sharps containers and wear gloves during procedures to ensure safety. Additionally, wear a lead apron in the fluoroscopy lounge to minimize radiation exposure.

rotations.html:
Dr. Diaz , D.O       

Integrative Spine and Sports

3308 NE 34th Street

Fort Lauderdale, FL 33308

Office Phone: (954)-564-3200 Fax: (954)-653-9188

Dr. Mark Fishman, DO

Dr. Francisco Romero, MD

South Florida Spine and Sports

3000 SW 148th Street Suite 115

Miramar, FL 33027

Office Phone: (954) 438-7000

Contact Info: Dr Fishman (Do not distribute) (954) 551-6921

Length:  average 3 Blocks, can vary

Dress: Scrubs

Schedule:

  • Tuesday: At Dr. Fishman/Dr. Romero’s office (one resident goes in at 8 am with Dr. Fishman, the other at 9 am with Dr. Romero, switching weekly).

  • Wednesday & Thursday: Switch on/off at the VA.

  • Friday: Both residents will be at Dr. Diaz’s office if an EMG is scheduled.

Responsibilities:

  • The goal of this rotation is for residents to familiarize themselves with EMG/NCS and learn how to perform basic studies. You are responsible for assisting, performing, and observing EMGs. The resident's role varies for each rotation site. The residents working on this rotation will need to work together to formulate a weekly schedule.

Additional Information:

  • For Dr. Fishman: You will observe studies during the rotation and review patient charts prior to the encounter.

  • For Dr. Romero: You will observe how to use an ultrasound (US). Throughout the course of your rotation block, he will escalate your duties accordingly, with the goal of having you scan patients independently by the end of the block.

  • ISS: The most important thing is to ensure the EMGs at Dr. Diaz’s office are covered. All residents on this rotation must be present on Friday. Please check WRS weekly and/or contact the residents currently working at Dr. Diaz’s office, typically each Thursday, to confirm if an EMG is scheduled for Friday morning, which is usually when EMGs are scheduled at ISS. If there is an EMG at Dr. Diaz’s office, that takes priority, even if it is on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, though this is unlikely. You will be responsible for performing the entire study and reviewing the results with Dr. Diaz. You will be expected to perform this NCS/EMG study independently, however, there is usually a senior resident at Dr. Diaz’s office who can assist you if necessary.

  • ISS Coverage: Due to the light schedule of this rotation, EMG rotators are often called in by ISS residents as necessary to help cover ISS. Residents working ISS will communicate with EMG residents accordingly.

  • WPB VA Coverage: When on the EMG rotation, residents may be asked to cover WBP VA on M, W, TH, or F (when an EMG is not scheduled at ISS). This is required in the instance of coverage demands and will be communicated to you in a timely manner by the chief resident.

Recommended Reading:

Liveson, Jay. Peripheral Neurology: Case Studies. Third Edition.

Preston DC, Shapiro BE. Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders, and Edition

Visco, Christopher J, Gary P Chimes, and James P McLean.  Mclean Course in Electrodiagnostic Medicine.

Weiss, Lyn D, J K. Silver, and Jay Weiss. Easy EMG: A Guide to Performing Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography.

Suggested Reading from American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine (AANEM):  http://www.aanem.org/Education/Resources/References/Suggested-Reading.aspx

The McLean Course in Electrodiagnostic Medicine Book is a good resident to resident guide on how to proceed in a stepwise fashion from the fundamentals to identifying, analyzing and performing the electrodiagnostic studies

QUICK REFERENCE

Site Attending Contact
ISS Jose Diaz, DO drjosejuandiaz@gmail.com
South Florida Spine & Sports Mark Fishman, MD; Francisco Romero, MD Office (954) 438-7000
WPB VA Jorge E. García-Negrón, MD and VA attendings jorge.garcia-negron2@va.gov

Core EDX skills to master

  • Motor NCS: median, ulnar, peroneal, tibial

  • Sensory NCS: median, ulnar, radial, sural, superficial peroneal

  • F-waves and H-reflexes; latency, amplitude and conduction velocity interpretation

  • Needle EMG: insertional and spontaneous activity (fibs, PSWs, CRDs, fasciculations), MUAP morphology, recruitment (early, reduced, discrete)

  • Key muscles for root, plexus and peripheral nerve localization

Common diagnoses

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome; ulnar neuropathy at the elbow

  • Cervical (C5–C8) and lumbosacral (L4–S1) radiculopathy

  • Length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetic)

  • Brachial and lumbosacral plexopathy

  • ALS / motor neuron disease red flags

Tips from residents

  • Start studying before the rotation; the learning curve is steep.

  • Cold limbs slow conduction: warm the patient first.

  • Always correlate EDX findings with the exam and imaging. Learn the common normal values.

  • Each site has a different EMG machine; get oriented on day 1 at each one.

  • The VA EMG section (above) has the weekly schedule, CPRS templates and lecture articles.

Attendings

Jose Diaz, DO

Mark Fishman, MD

Francisco Romero, MD
