Length: 3 Months

Attending(s): Kester J. Nedd, D.O.

Contact: MA/Soraya will likely reach out 2 weeks in advance by email/phone. Be sure to check your Larkin email. If she does not, reach out using the number provided to make them aware you will be starting. They will do orientation on the first day you start on how to use their office EMR, put in orders and code for billing.

Contact number:

Dr. Kester Nedd (c) (305) 588- 3314 (Please don’t share)

Dr. Michael A Wilson (954)-296-1661

Soraya (resident coordinator at the office - person to reach for schedule and PTO forms) (786)-348-2124

Jaklyn (305)-479-8724

Time (hours, days): You will be primarily working with Dr. Nedd. Wednesday/Thursdays are Dr. Nedd’s clinic days usually. Dr Nedd sometimes changes his clinic days. You are expected to be there on Wednesday/Thursdays regardless if Dr. Nedd has clinic or not. If Dr Nedd does not have clinic, you will be working with Dr. Wilson.

For outpatient: Soraya, who is the resident coordinator will reach out with Dr. Nedd’s and Dr. Wilson’s schedule a week or two before you start. If she does not, contact her at least a week in advance using the number above. Their clinic runs Mon-Fri with Dr. Nedd working usually Wed and Thurs. The other days are Dr. Wilson’s clinic days (Mon, Tues, Fri). However, this is not set in stone so be sure to get the schedule from Soraya. You are exempt on didactics days, so Mondays and usually third Thurs of the month. On your first day, arrive at the clinic at 9AM, unless Sorya tells you otherwise. Someone from the office, if not Soraya, will go over how to use EMR, put in orders, and code for billing as well as give you your personal username/password for EMR access. There are usually Optho, Psych and Neuro residents there as well. Their day to day schedule start and end times vary (see the schedule from the MA/Soraya), but expect to start at 9AM with both attendings and as late as 4-5PM with Dr. Wilson. However, with Dr. Nedd, expect to be at the clinic until 11PM-12AM. You usually start your day at 9AM with in person visits followed by seeing telehealth patients in between patients in which you will see the patient, write your note, present to the attending, see the patient together with the attending, and then finish your notes. All notes and orders have to be submitted before leaving. Do NOT sign any of the notes, simply save/pend them. Bring your own laptop for the clinic as there are limited computers in the office with the number of residents/med students. It is also easier/more efficient for you to write the notes while you are talking to the patient versus seeing the patient and then going to one of the desktops to write your notes.

Dress: Scrubs

Locations:

Design Neuroscience Center (address above)

Recommended Reading: TBI (Zasler)

Miscellaneous: Parking is available outside DNC.

Food: Some days reps will bring lunch at DNC

Attending Michael Wilson, MD (954) 296-1661

Office staff Jaklyn (305) 479-8724

  • Acquired brain injury and TBI; disorders of consciousness (CRS-R, FOUR score) and prognosis

  • Spasticity ladder: stretching → oral agents → focal chemodenervation → intrathecal baclofen

rotations.title: Pediatric PM&R/ PED I
rotations.html:
Nationwide Children’s Hospital

700 Children's Dr, Columbus, OH 43205

Contact: Leah Settles leah.settles@nationwidechildrens.org (coordinator): Contact 1 month prior to rotating. She will provide you with parking and orientation information as well as a schedule.

Epic/Pacs/IT department: 614-355-3750.

Helpful files (sample schedule, maps, Castro Housing Application) can be found in the google drive or click here. Or fill out here online https://www.castocommunities.com/apply-now/

Length: 1 Month

Attending(s): Michelle Miller, M.D.

Apartment: Please reach out to our coordinator (2026 Coordinator is currently Carola Rodriguez) to book your flight and living accommodations. Do not assume that this will be all set up by the time your rotation starts. It is your onus of duty to ensure everything is complete including your living accommodations, orientation etc

Schedule: Monday - Friday 8am - 5pm

Dress: Professional Attire, no white coat.

From the residents: Attendance is required on the 1st of the month for orientation, residents will be excused from their rotation in the month prior 2 days early to allow time to travel. Two days will also be excused when the rotation is completed for travel. These days will NOT count as PTO but please ensure your attending and chiefs are aware that you will be absent.

The attendings are amazing and they mean it when they say our education is their first priority. The attendings all switch duties, from inpatient, outpatient and consults. You'll be able to work with everyone eventually, wherever they're placed. Some hold informal lectures during lunch and will let you know about them.

There are OSU PM&R residents here too. A PGY-2 is assigned only to inpatient and a PGY-3 is assigned only to outpatient. We split our days to do both inpatient and outpatient- they want us to be well rounded. At inpatient I'm capped at 3 patients (doesn't sound like much but it's actually reasonable) so that I can finish notes and follow up on things before the clinic in the afternoon. At clinic there are multiple attendings working- so plenty of patients for me and the PGY-3 OSU resident to share. There is a multidisciplinary clinic for myelodysplasia and CP. There are also designated days for concussion clinic and Botox procedures. EMG's are also done, and you can participate in those if you have interest.

Competency:

Become acquainted with and comfortable in treatment (therapies, medications, and orthotics) used in treatment of the pediatric population. Your responsibilities are minimal at best with this rotation, so please take the time to read up on their pathologies, observe their deficits, and recognize the stark difference between elderly care vs. pediatric care.

Reading Material:

PM&R Pocketpedia, Cuccurullo

PTO- Reach out to leah.settles@nationwidechildrens.org. You need all signatures from Chiefs, Diaz and the attendings at Nation wide

Clinic locations while at Nationwide and Map.

(They will send a map with part of onboarding, but does not include details)

Inpatient unit (H9b): When you enter through the main entrance, take a right, you’ll look for the hallway that has lockers in it, you’ll need to badge through this door into the employee hallway. Then you will take a left and walk down the hall to the third set of elevators (it’s further than you think and it is a three elevators in this area). Take elevator to 9th floor where you will find the inpatient rehabilitation unit.

  • You will split the census with the OSU PM&R resident

General/ Concussion/ Botox/ NATBI (non accidental TBI) clinics: are all in the PM&R clinic on the first floor of hospital T1a clinic across from urgent care.

  • For general/concussion, you will be asked to see patients and write notes on a few patients each clinic under guidance of attending

  • NATBI, often multidisciplinary with PM&R/Psychology/social worker

  • Depends on who you work with and how many days you have with them, they may allow you to assist with Botox injections

Myelo Clinic is all the way at end of hospital near the orange garage

  • Multidisciplinary clinic - you will typically follow a patient in order to be able to see all the different care plans for each of the specialties. (PM&R, neurosurgery, GI, urology, PT/OT, social work, Etc.)

EMG H10a, on the 10th floor on the A side (floor above the inpatient rehab unit but on the opposite side). When you walk through the double doors, to the right is a workstation looking area with a door into the EMG room.

  • Only if scheduled, may be a patient or two, and then be asked to go to another clinic after

Cerebral Palsy (CP) clinic and Seating clinic are in the ORTHO building (LOSC). C is on the 5th floor. Seating clinic is on 2nd floor.

If not ubering directly there, there is a garage you can park at if driving, or walk from the main hospital (about 7 minute walk). Enter the building on the north side of LOSC building as there is no entrance directly from Livingston ave.

  • CP clinic is also multidisciplinary clinic - (PM&R, ortho, neurosurgery, PT/OT, social work, Etc.)

  • Seating clinic is with attending, PT, and seating company.

MAIN HOSPITAL Map

HOSPITAL COMPLEX: how to get to LOSC building from main hospital

QUICK REFERENCE

Role Name Contact
Pediatric PM&R Attending Michelle A. Miller, MD through Leah Settles
Rotation Coordinator (Nationwide) Leah Settles leah.settles@nationwidechildrens.org
Epic / PACS / IT — (614) 355-3750
Travel and housing (Larkin) Program coordinator (Carola Rodriguez in 2026) Larkin GME

Inpatient rehab (H9B): From the main entrance turn right to the hallway with lockers, badge through the door into the employee hallway, turn left and continue to the third set of elevators (farther than you expect). Take them to the 9th floor.

Common diagnoses

  • Cerebral palsy (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, mixed); GMFCS, MACS and CFCS levels

  • Spina bifida / myelomeningocele

  • Duchenne and other muscular dystrophies

  • Pediatric TBI, acquired brain injury and stroke

  • Brachial plexus birth palsy

  • Down syndrome and other chromosomal disorders; pediatric sports injuries

Tips from residents

  • Parents and guardians are the main historians; involve them in every conversation.

  • Botulinum toxin dosing in children is weight-based and very different from adults.

  • Out-of-state credentialing takes longer; contact Leah Settles early.

Attendings

Michelle A. Miller, MD

Inpatient unit (H9b): When you enter through the main entrance, take a right, you’ll look for the hallway that has lockers in it, you’ll need to badge through this door into the employee hallway. Then you will take a left and walk down the hall to the third set of elevators (it’s further than you think and it is a three elevators in this area). Take elevator to 9th floor where you will find the inpatient rehabilitation unit.

  • You will split the census with the OSU PM&R resident

General/ Concussion/ Botox/ NATBI (non accidental TBI) clinics: are all in the PM&R clinic on the first floor of hospital T1a clinic across from urgent care.

  • For general/concussion, you will be asked to see patients and write notes on a few patients each clinic under guidance of attending

  • NATBI, often multidisciplinary with PM&R/Psychology/social worker

  • Depends on who you work with and how many days you have with them, they may allow you to assist with Botox injections

Myelo Clinic is all the way at end of hospital near the orange garage

  • Multidisciplinary clinic - you will typically follow a patient in order to be able to see all the different care plans for each of the specialties. (PM&R, neurosurgery, GI, urology, PT/OT, social work, Etc.)

EMG H10a, on the 10th floor on the A side (floor above the inpatient rehab unit but on the opposite side). When you walk through the double doors, to the right is a workstation looking area with a door into the EMG room.

  • Only if scheduled, may be a patient or two, and then be asked to go to another clinic after

Cerebral Palsy (CP) clinic and Seating clinic are in the ORTHO building (LOSC). C is on the 5th floor. Seating clinic is on 2nd floor.

If not ubering directly there, there is a garage you can park at if driving, or walk from the main hospital (about 7 minute walk). Enter the building on the north side of LOSC building as there is no entrance directly from Livingston ave.

  • CP clinic is also multidisciplinary clinic - (PM&R, ortho, neurosurgery, PT/OT, social work, Etc.)

  • Seating clinic is with attending, PT, and seating company.

MAIN HOSPITAL Map

HOSPITAL COMPLEX: how to get to LOSC building from main hospital

Role Name Contact
Pediatric PM&R Attending Michelle A. Miller, MD through Leah Settles
Rotation Coordinator (Nationwide) Leah Settles leah.settles@nationwidechildrens.org
Epic / PACS / IT — (614) 355-3750
Travel and housing (Larkin) Program coordinator (Carola Rodriguez in 2026) Larkin GME

Inpatient rehab (H9B): From the main entrance turn right to the hallway with lockers, badge through the door into the employee hallway, turn left and continue to the third set of elevators (farther than you expect). Take them to the 9th floor.

Common diagnoses

  • Cerebral palsy (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, mixed); GMFCS, MACS and CFCS levels

  • Spina bifida / myelomeningocele

  • Duchenne and other muscular dystrophies

  • Pediatric TBI, acquired brain injury and stroke

  • Brachial plexus birth palsy

  • Down syndrome and other chromosomal disorders; pediatric sports injuries

Tips from residents

  • Parents and guardians are the main historians; involve them in every conversation.

  • Botulinum toxin dosing in children is weight-based and very different from adults.

  • Out-of-state credentialing takes longer; contact Leah Settles early.

Michelle A. Miller, MD

Website: www.apccfl.com; https://drhatgis.com/

Length: 1 Block

Attending(s): Jesse Hatgis, DO

Contact: Contact Dr. Hatgis 1 month prior to elective rotation via email

Time (hours, days): Monday-Friday @ Tamarac Office for Clinic 8:00 AM - 5:00pm with procedures on Friday AM.

  • Clinic with Hatgis on M/Th/F, work with the PAs on T/W

  • New surgery center is currently awaiting certification by an accrediting body, Lauderdale Lakes Surgical center is no longer accepting residents or Fellows to observe or participate in procedures at all.

Dress: Matching scrubs. White coat optional during clinic hours.

Locations: Interventional Spine Specialists (7171 N University Dr. Suite 300, Tamarac, FL 33321)

Recommended Reading: Braddom PM&R Chapters 25, 37, 40. Read about transforaminal, interlaminar, and caudal epidurals as well as medial branch blocks, facet joint injections, rhizotomies, spinal cord stimulator implants, PRP, and discograms. Atlas of Image-Guided Spinal Procedures by Michael Furman

Responsibilities: Arrive on time during clinic and outpatient surgery days. Read and stay engaged with patient visits and procedures. You will observe patient visits and procedures with Dr. Hatgis in clinic. Get familiar with low back pain treatment algorithms from PAs. DO NOT spend too much time with patients, the MAs will gather a brief history to report to you and you can confirm it with the patient, then do a short focused physical exam and tell patient likely plan, then present to PA/Hatgis and you will all go in together to give final plan to the patient.Once comfortable with anatomy and spine knowledge, Dr. Hatgis will let you assist with procedures including medial branch blocks and epidural injections. You will also have exposure to facet, sacroiliac, epidural injections under fluoroscopy and lots of advanced procedures including spinal cord stimulation, peripheral nerve stimulation, endoscopic rhizotomy, minimally invasive lumbar decompression, and regenerative modalities. Maintain procedure log.

QUICK REFERENCE

Procedures you may see

  • Medial branch blocks, facet injections, rhizotomy (including endoscopic)

  • Epidurals: transforaminal, interlaminar, caudal

  • Spinal cord stimulator implants; peripheral nerve stimulation; MILD procedure

  • PRP injections; discograms

Attendings

Jesse Hatgis, DO

rotations.html:
Electives

Responsibilities: Discuss Elective with Dr. Diaz at least 2 months in advance. Approval contingent on Dr. Diaz and GME.

Required documentation: Elective / Selective Form, available at GME at Larkin. If attempting out-of-state rotation you will need to apply for temporary resident training license in that state, arrange to complete that paperwork as early as possible in the planning process because this takes time. PLAs generally take about 1 month to complete, submit paperwork for elective form as early as possible to prevent delays in start time.

Rheumatology

Location:

Arthritis Specialists

9750 NW 33rd St. #204

Coral Springs, FL33065

Attending:

Barry Waters, MD

954-341-5034

Office Hours:

M-F 8:00 – 4:00

Contact office 1 week prior to starting rotation.

Dr. Waters will see mostly patients with RA, OA, osteoporosis, and HLA B-27 Seronegative Spondylarthropathies. Please read rheumatology chapter in Braddom 5th Edition prior to rotation.

Dress professionally with white coat, be on time, and complete all notes prior to leaving his office.

You can either use an office laptop or bring your own laptop computer for access to his EMR. Residents will go into the room with either new/follow up patients and take an adequate history and physical. Formulate your assessment and plan and present the case to Dr. Waters. You guys will then see the patient together and finish the note with the recommendations.

Dr. Waters loves to teach and he will often ask you lots of questions. Please be willing learn and ask questions. Once a week you will join the rheumatology fellows for their didactics. At the end of the rotation you will be required to give a presentation at their didactics.

Meals are not provided however his office usually has food from drug reps.

9 a.m. – 5 p.m.

Monday-Friday

Responsibilities: Arrive early, leave late. See patients with attending. You will observe procedures with Dr. Davis and can assist with rhizotomys. You will observe patient visits and procedures with Dr. Roa and can assist with rhizotomys. Once comfortable, Dr. Roa will let you assist with more procedures. Every other Tuesday morning Dr. Davis does procedures at the Weston Outpatient Surgery Center which is good to see other procedures.

Advanced Orthopedics

www.advancedhere.com

Additional Offices: Altamonte Springs, Orlando, Tampa, Sarasota, Ft Myers, Ft Pierce, Port St Lucie, Palm Beach Gardens, Boca Raton, Hollywood & Miami

Length: 1 month

Attending(s): Drs. Barry E. Schapiro, Scott S. Katzman, Jeffrey H. Oppenheimer, Denise Andrade (PA), LewJack Dorance (PA)

Contact: Call the Hollywood Office – (954) 987-2047 – and speak to the office manager a minimum of two weeks in advance. REQUIRED documentation to be submitted prior to the rotation are Weston Surgical Center Supervision Agreement, CV, BLS, ACLS plus any other documents as per the office. Florida Medical Center Requires Human Resource Orientation for a badge. Complete prior to the rotation you may expect half day orientation.

Time (hours, days): Monday to Friday. Contact office and ask for start time. Each day is different depending on whether or not Dr. Schapiro is doing surgery that day, or which office he is going to that day.

Dress: Scrubs, white coat and name badge.

Locations: The main outpatient offices you will be at is the Hollywood Office and the Boca Raton office. Weston Surgical Center, Florida Medical Center, Memorial Hospital, possibly other surgical centers as per Dr. Schapiro. Dr. Schapiro sometimes goes to an office in Orlando, and going up with him is optional.

Recommended Reading: Anatomy Text. Braddom PM&R Chapters: Chapters 1, 24, 38, 39, 44. This is a good rotation to learn how to read spine MRI and X-rays of spine, shoulders and knees. Take advantage and ask plenty of questions.

Responsibilities: Arrive on time, as per instructions from the office. See patients independently and with attending. Write out paper SOAP notes to assist attending in dictations. Prepare for surgeries by reading the night before. Assist in preOp, taking the patient to the OR, setting up the patient in the OR, scrub for surgeries and assist as per Dr. Schapiro request.

Additional Information: Multiple procedures possible, such as shoulder and knee injections. You will also have some exposure to facet and hip injections under fluoroscopy. Maintain procedure log. Ask your attending prior to performing OMT. You may perform OMT on the appropriate patient/condition.

policies.title: Coverage & Departure Protocol
policies.html:
In order to maintain a professional and organized working environment, it is essential for residents to adhere to the following protocol regarding their departure from the workplace:

  • Attending Dismissal Requirement: Residents must be formally dismissed by the attending physician before leaving their assigned duties for the day. Walking out without proper dismissal is not permitted.

By following this protocol, we ensure that all patient care responsibilities are adequately covered and that there is clear communication within the medical team.

policies.title: Didactics Attendance Policy
policies.html:
Residents must be present for 80% of scheduled didactic sessions for the year (not counting documented excused absences for PTO/Sick Days/Bereavement or time on elective rotation). If a session is scheduled for in person - the resident must be present in person at the start of the session. Plan accordingly and arrive early for Monday rotations so that you can complete your clinical responsibilities and arrive on time for didactics. It is required that you attend and actively participate in the entirety of the didactic lecture. You must be present in person for in person sessions if you are not on approved PTO or currently on the VA or Ohio Pediatrics Rotation. Attendance will be monitored and those who are repeatedly tardy or absent will be notified with potential consequences for continued absences including but not limited to: loss of PTO, moonlighting privileges, and formal academic probation. If you are running late, please notify chiefs in a timely manner so that you are not marked tardy/absent. If you are repeatedly tardy you may be marked absent for the session.

  • Nationwide Children’s Hospital: Attendance will be excused during this one month rotation.

  • WPB VA: Attendance at didactics while on this rotations is required. Attendance will be taken based on your presence in the video conference call. Failure to attend and actively participate will result in a recorded absence.

  • Elective Rotations: Residents on elective rotations are excused from attending didactic sessions for the month they are on elective.

policies.title: PTO Policy
policies.html: Residents must submit completed PTO/CME request form 30 days prior to dates off service. PTO form must have the attending and coresident signature present to be accepted. Coresident coverage is mandatory for all rotations for you to take PTO. Please submit completed PTO forms to the larkin chief email. PTO will be formally tracked and if you are found to be absent from work without approved paperwork it will be treated as a professionalism concern and potential consequences include loss of PTO, disciplinary sanctions, and/or extension of training. If you are out sick, please text your attending on service ASAP so that they are aware. PTO form noting sick day should be submitted on the first day back on service after illness. All general policies from Larkin GME must be followed for taking PTO - refer to resident handbook for details. No more than 5 PTO days may be taken per month without prior approval from Dr. Diaz. Do not request PTO at the start of the week on a new inpatient service as it may not be approved.

policies.title: FMLA & Leave Policies
policies.html:
All general policies from Larkin GME must be followed for taking FMLA:

Residents considering leave requests under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) will be permitted to take leave if they meet the requirements outlined in the Employee Policy regarding FMLA. Residents must provide at least thirty (30) days’ notice when the leave is foreseeable, or as much notice as practical when it is not, and must complete all forms required by the sponsoring institution’s Graduate Medical Education Office and Human Resources Department before going on leave.

Paternity Leave: After the delivery of a resident’s spouse, the resident may take a maximum of five (5) days of parental leave during the postpartum period. These five days include weekends and holidays and may begin either on the day of delivery or on the day of discharge from the hospital after birth. Responsibility for night call is not waived unless coverage is arranged. This leave must be approved by the Program Director and the Designated Institutional Official (DIO) and will be counted against personal/optional leave time.

Maternity Leave: Residents who give birth will be granted a total of twelve (12) calendar weeks of maternity leave. Of these twelve weeks, six (6) weeks will be paid and six (6) weeks will be unpaid. Maternity leave applies only in cases where the resident is physically having a baby. Use of this leave must be coordinated with the GME Office and Human Resources, and documentation must include a physician’s certificate indicating the approximate due date. The Program Director will determine how much time, if any, must be made up in order to meet Specialty Board Certification and individual Review Committee requirements.

Family Grievance Leave:

In addition to GME policies, residents are also subject to the policies and procedures set forth in the sponsoring institution’s Human Resources Policies and Procedures Manual.

policies.title: Grievances & Due Process
policies.html:
PURPOSE: To provide residents with reasonable written institutional policies and procedures for Grievance and Due process.

This disciplinary process does not generate a contractual obligation on the part of the sponsoring institution to use progressive discipline in all cases. The sponsoring institution has the right to discipline any inappropriate conduct without being required to progress through these levels of discipline.

This document will be provided to the residents prior to the beginning of each training year within the

residency manual. These policies will minimize any conflict of interest by adjudicating parties in addressing academic or other disciplinary actions taken against residents that could result in dismissal, non-renewal of a resident’s agreement, non-promotion of a resident to the next level of training, or other actions that could significantly threaten a resident’s intended career, negotiation of resident complaints related to the work environment or issues related to the program or faculty.

DEFINITIONS

A. Designated Institutional Official (DIO): The physician who has the responsibility for the oversight, administration and accountability of residency programs.

B. Administrative Director of Medical Education (ADME): Responsible for managing administrative functions of the GME Division reporting to the Sponsoring Institution governing body.

C. Department Chairperson: The individual responsible for administrative, clinical and academic affairs of a clinical department.

D. The Graduate Medical Education Committee (GMEC) comprises the Chairman of the GMEC, Designated Institutional Officer (DIO), Administrative Director of Graduate Medical Education (ADME), Residency Program Directors, Peer Selected Residents Representatives, Faculty Representatives at base institution and local participating sites, and representatives from administration (i.e. CEO/CEO Designee and COO).

E. The Disciplinary Committee: A standing committee of the Graduate Medical Education Committee comprised by the same members. The Vice President of Legal Affairs may serve as a counselor for the Disciplinary Committee. This committee has the responsibility to review recommendations from a department regarding extensions of Concern Status, Probation, and Termination, subject to the limitations set forth in this policy.

F. Program Director: The physician responsible to manage a residency program.

G. Resident/Intern/Fellow = Trainee: A physician in training under contract with the sponsoring institution who is enrolled in one of the training programs.

H. Supervising Attending Physician: An attending physician who is responsible for the performance of the Resident for a particular service.

Types of Progressive Discipline

Coaching: this is a non-threatening conversation between the resident and resident supervising Attending Physician which is intended to improve overall performance or professional conduct and behavior. The resident Supervising Physician may use coaching when work performance, academic performance or other work-related conduct is not satisfactory. During a coaching session, a supervising attending physician should point out the instances of inappropriate conduct or academic deficits, suggest corrective action, and ask for the resident for an agreement to change.

Oral counseling: this is a first level of notice of a manner of disciplinary concern, which may be taken by the supervising attending physician. If a resident continues to engage in similar inappropriate conduct or if the resident’s conduct is such that bypassing coaching is justified, the supervising physician may engage in oral counseling. Oral counseling constitutes a warning. A discussion should be held between the supervising Attending Physician and the resident. The supervising attending physician should advice the resident of the problem, point out specific instances of the problem, and suggest appropriate corrective action. The discussion should be mutual and should focus on problem solving. The supervising attending physician would advise the resident that he/she is expected to not repeat the problem behavior and that more severe disciplinary action will be taken if the behavior recurs.

Written Reprimand: this is a more serious and a higher level of discipline which may be taken by the Supervising Physician or Program Director; which should be in writing and should include the following:

1. Trainee name;

2. Person(s) present at the meeting in which the Supervising Physician or Program Director gives the written reprimand to the trainee;

3. The reason for the reprimand;

4. A brief description of the incident or conduct that lead to the reprimand;

5. The dates, times, and location of the conduct for which trainee is being reprimanded;

6. The dates of prior discipline regarding such conduct and any corrective action;

7. A signature line for the trainee, Supervising Attending Physician, Program Director, and a copy to the DIO.

By signing the written reprimand, the trainee is acknowledging receipt of the document. If the resident refuses the sign the document, the program director should make that notation on the document, sign and date it. The document may include a monitoring period, state the standards for judging the resident’s improvement and how often the resident will be evaluated.

Concern Status: this is a level of formal discipline less serious than Probation. A resident may be placed on Concern Status by the Program Director for a period of up to 6 months. The Program Director is required to notify the Department Chair or Graduate Medical Education Committee. The Program Director must notify the Chair of Department and to the DIO. These representatives will notify the Disciplinary Committee in writing of placement of a trainee on concern status. Any extensions thereof or move to probation status requires approval of the Disciplinary Committee.

Types of concern status:

1. Clinical concern includes unsatisfactory performance on the clinical portions of the resident’s program.

2. Academic concern includes unsatisfactory performance on the knowledge-based portions of the resident’s program.

3. Professional concern includes behaviors, which call into question the clinical, personal or moral attributes of the resident as they relate to fitness to practice of medicine. During the period of concern status, the Program Director shall evaluate the resident monthly, shall inform the resident in writing of the deficiencies and expectations for remediation concern status, and may remove resident from such status by written with copies sent to the DIO. These representatives or the Program Director must also notify the Disciplinary Committee.

Probation: Probation period of critical examination of a resident to determine if he/she may continue in the program. Probation may be preceded by a concern status but may be imposed without such prior discipline if warranted by the seriousness of the precipitating circumstance. Probation may be imposed for up to 3 months by the Disciplinary Committee and may be extended for additional periods by the Disciplinary Committee upon recommendation of the Program Director, DIO. Any extended probation status shall be reviewed at the end of each rotation by the Disciplinary Committee. Program Director or designee shall evaluate the resident monthly and inform the resident in writing of the deficiencies and expectations and may remove the resident from such status by written notice with copies sent to the Disciplinary Committee.

Termination for Cause: The Disciplinary Committee may decide the termination of a trainee from a trainee training program or the termination of a trainee contract for any of the reasons or causes set forth in the trainee physician employment contract or as set forth below. The Program Director, in collaboration of the Disciplinary Committee, may terminate a trainee from the training program or terminate the trainee contract.

Disciplinary Decisions and the Disciplinary Committee: A resident’s Supervising Physician may coach a Trainee and give oral counseling. Written reprimands to a Trainee shall involve the Program Director, who may place a concern status. If such a determination is made for a period greater than 6 months it requires approval of the disciplinary committee, which will make the decisions regarding extensions of Concern Status, Probation, and recommendations of

Termination as follows: The Program Director may write recommendations to the Disciplinary Committee which has the authority to adopt, disapprove or modify said recommendation from a program director to take disciplinary action and shall advise the DIO of its decisions. If that decision is to recommend termination of a resident, the DIO will have final authority as to whether to terminate the resident from the training program and/or terminate the resident’s contract, after the proper steps of discipline have been conducted appropriately. During the period of any extension of Concern Status or Probation, the Program Director or Designee shall evaluate the resident monthly, shall inform the resident in writing of the deficiencies and expectations; and may remove the resident from such status by written notice.

DISCIPLINARY DECISIONS AND THE DISCIPLINARY COMMITTEE

· During the period of any extension of Concern Status or Probation, the Program Director will evaluate the trainee monthly, inform the trainee in writing of the deficiencies and expectations; and may remove the trainee from such status by written notice.

Disciplinary Actions which are appealable are:

· Coaching – is not appealable under the policy, and is not subject to appeal.

· Oral counseling, written reprimand, placement on concern status (clinical, academic or professional ) and Probation & Extension: Oral Warning, Written Reprimand, Placement on Concern Status and Probation may be discussed by “Informal Dispute” pursuant to the policy but are not appealable.

· Termination of trainee from intern/residency training program or employment contract for cause: is separate and distinct from others forms of discipline and is the only level which may be appealed. Prohibition against Retaliation: The sponsoring institution is committed to preventing any retaliation against persons who may raise legitimate questions regarding their employment in good faith. Supervisors are expected to take the time to answer questions, and work toward the resolution of workplace concerns. Doing so will make an important contribution to the overall performance and growth of this organization.

TERMINATION- see Larkin manual

· Oral counseling, written reprimand, placement on concern status (clinical, academic or professional ) and Probation & Extension: Oral Warning, Written Reprimand, Placement on Concern Status and Probation may be discussed by “Informal Dispute” pursuant to the policy but are not appealable.

· Termination of trainee from intern/residency training program or employment contract for cause: is separate and distinct from others forms of discipline and is the only level which may be appealed. Prohibition against Retaliation: The sponsoring institution is committed to preventing any retaliation against persons who may raise legitimate questions regarding their employment in good faith. Supervisors are expected to take the time to answer questions, and work toward the resolution of workplace concerns. Doing so will make an important contribution to the overall performance and growth of this organization.

TERMINATION- see Larkin manual

guides.name: Electrodiagnostics (EDX) - EMG Rotation
guides.html:
ELECTRODIAGNOSTICS

Dr. Diaz , D.O       

Integrative Spine and Sports

3308 NE 34th Street

Fort Lauderdale, FL 33308

Office Phone: (954)-564-3200 Fax: (954)-653-9188

Dr. Mark Fishman, DO

Dr. Francisco Romero, MD

South Florida Spine and Sports

3000 SW 148th Street Suite 115

Miramar, FL 33027

Office Phone: (954) 438-7000

Contact Info: Dr Fishman (Do not distribute) (954) 551-6921

Length:  average 3 Blocks, can vary

Dress: Scrubs

Schedule:

  • Tuesday: At Dr. Fishman/Dr. Romero’s office (one resident goes in at 8 am with Dr. Fishman, the other at 9 am with Dr. Romero, switching weekly).

    Wednesday & Thursday: Switch on/off at the VA.

    Friday: Both residents will be at Dr. Diaz’s office if an EMG is scheduled.

Responsibilities:

  • The goal of this rotation is for residents to familiarize themselves with EMG/NCS and learn how to perform basic studies. You are responsible for assisting, performing, and observing EMGs. The resident's role varies for each rotation site. The residents working on this rotation will need to work together to formulate a weekly schedule.

Additional Information:

  • For Dr. Fishman: You will observe studies during the rotation and review patient charts prior to the encounter.

    For Dr. Romero: You will observe how to use an ultrasound (US). Throughout the course of your rotation block, he will escalate your duties accordingly, with the goal of having you scan patients independently by the end of the block.

    ISS: The most important thing is to ensure the EMGs at Dr. Diaz’s office are covered. All residents on this rotation must be present on Friday. Please check WRS weekly and/or contact the residents currently working at Dr. Diaz’s office, typically each Thursday, to confirm if an EMG is scheduled for Friday morning, which is usually when EMGs are scheduled at ISS. If there is an EMG at Dr. Diaz’s office, that takes priority, even if it is on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, though this is unlikely. You will be responsible for performing the entire study and reviewing the results with Dr. Diaz. You will be expected to perform this NCS/EMG study independently, however, there is usually a senior resident at Dr. Diaz’s office who can assist you if necessary.

    ISS Coverage: Due to the light schedule of this rotation, EMG rotators are often called in by ISS residents as necessary to help cover ISS. Residents working ISS will communicate with EMG residents accordingly.

    WPB VA Coverage: When on the EMG rotation, residents may be asked to cover WBP VA on M, W, TH, or F (when an EMG is not scheduled at ISS). This is required in the instance of coverage demands and will be communicated to you in a timely manner by the chief resident.

Recommended Reading:

Liveson, Jay. Peripheral Neurology: Case Studies. Third Edition.

Preston DC, Shapiro BE. Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders, and Edition

Visco, Christopher J, Gary P Chimes, and James P McLean.  Mclean Course in Electrodiagnostic Medicine.

Weiss, Lyn D, J K. Silver, and Jay Weiss. Easy EMG: A Guide to Performing Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography.

Suggested Reading from American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine (AANEM):  http://www.aanem.org/Education/Resources/References/Suggested-Reading.aspx

The McLean Course in Electrodiagnostic Medicine Book is a good resident to resident guide on how to proceed in a stepwise fashion from the fundamentals to identifying, analyzing and performing the electrodiagnostic studies

QUICK REFERENCE

Site Attending Contact
ISS Jose Diaz, DO drjosejuandiaz@gmail.com
South Florida Spine & Sports Mark Fishman, MD; Francisco Romero, MD Office (954) 438-7000
WPB VA Jorge E. García-Negrón, MD and VA attendings jorge.garcia-negron2@va.gov

Core EDX skills to master

  • Motor NCS: median, ulnar, peroneal, tibial

    Sensory NCS: median, ulnar, radial, sural, superficial peroneal

    F-waves and H-reflexes; latency, amplitude and conduction velocity interpretation

    Needle EMG: insertional and spontaneous activity (fibs, PSWs, CRDs, fasciculations), MUAP morphology, recruitment (early, reduced, discrete)

    Key muscles for root, plexus and peripheral nerve localization

Common diagnoses

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome; ulnar neuropathy at the elbow

    Cervical (C5–C8) and lumbosacral (L4–S1) radiculopathy

    Length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetic)

    Brachial and lumbosacral plexopathy

    ALS / motor neuron disease red flags

Tips from residents

  • Start studying before the rotation; the learning curve is steep.

    Cold limbs slow conduction: warm the patient first.

    Always correlate EDX findings with the exam and imaging. Learn the common normal values.

    Each site has a different EMG machine; get oriented on day 1 at each one.

    The VA EMG section (above) has the weekly schedule, CPRS templates and lecture articles.

Attendings

Jose Diaz, DO

Mark Fishman, MD

Francisco Romero, MD

WEST PALM BEACH VA MEDICAL CENTER

Outpatient PM&R Rotation

West Palm Beach Veterans Affairs Medical

7305 N Military Trl, West Palm Beach, FL 33410

Length: 3-4 month block

Attending:

Jorge Enrique García-Negrón, MD Chief, WPB VAMC PM&R

Srinivas Reddy, MD WPB VAMC PM&R Staff Physician

Francisco J. Garcia, MD WPB VAMC PM&R Staff Physician

Jeremy Fitzig, DO WPB VAMC PM&R Staff Physician

Contact:   

Jorge Garcia-Negron: jorge.garcia-negron2@va.gov

Medical Education Coordinator

Kendra Morris: Kendra.Morris@va.gov

Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation Service

West Palm Beach VA Medical Center

7305 N. Military Trail, PM&RS (117)

West Palm Beach, FL  33418

Dress: Scrubs and VA PIV card.

Scheduling: M-F (some days are heavier EMG than others) time spent with clinic and EMG/NCS

Responsibilities:

  • Clinic daily (US guided procedures, PRP, Botox/Spasticity, TBI, P&O, Wheelchair, Prolotherapy, Spinal procedures) and EMG’s during mornings (+ a few afternoons). Multiple procedures possible. Maintain procedure log.  If appropriate, ask your attending prior to performing OMT.  Also, there are many enthusiastic attendings on the WPB VA PM&R team that are interested in lecturing.  They will be contributing to LCH PM&R didactics.

    Become well acquainted with Neurodiagnostic equipment, tools, understanding of anatomy, and how to use EDX in practice.

    PGY 4 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day with the exception of didactic sessions (typically held Monday and the third Thursday of the month from 2-6p).

    PGY 3 residents are expected to attend work at the VA for 8 hours per day 1-2 days a week. They both attend once per week at minimum for EMGs.

Attendance:

  • At the VA, the resident’s attendance will be kept track of by PGY4 seniors and Dr Reid at the end of each rotation month. This will be emailed to Kendra Morris and tracked. A copy of all PTO and coverage forms should be printed and given to Dr. Reid for her records. All attendings and co-residents should be notified in advance for PTO.

    PTO: To be signed by Dr. Reid within the first week of the rotation - negotiable during the rotation.

    Larkin Community Hospital (LCH) will monitor attendance by tracking PTO forms (copy of each is available from the program coordinator). A calendar or list will also be kept by the PMR chief resident.

    In the EMG room, there is a maximum capacity for 3 PMR residents. This is generally, 2 PGY4 residents from LCH and 1 PMR resident from Broward Health North (BHN). If there are 3 PGY4 residents from LCH scheduled at the same time, they will alternate fairly to the outpatient clinic to maintain 3 residents total in the EMG room.

    When a LCH PGY-3 resident joins the EMG rotation on Wednesdays and Thursdays, one-two of the LCH PGY-4 residents or BHN resident currently in EMG will be expected to voluntarily transition to the outpatient clinic to maintain appropriate staffing. The resident transitioning to the outpatient clinic should alternate fairly between LCH and BHN.

    Fluoroscopy Suite Restriction: Please note that residents will not be permitted to rotate through the fluoroscopy suite during the upcoming academic year until further notice.

    PGY 3 residents may be asked to cover shifts, and a PTO form will be required with their signature, on the days that do not interfere with other parts of their rotation (coverage should not interfere with Dr. Fishman/Dr. Romero (Tues) or Dr. Diaz (Fri when there are EMGs)).

    Of the 4 residents on EMG/ISS and the VA there should be no overlapping PTO unless there are extenuating circumstances.

Didactic Attendance: Virtual attendance is required.

West Palm VA EMG Article presentation: Dr. Reid will assign an article to present and work with all residents to schedule a time during lunch (usually Tuesdays and Fridays).

Recommended Reading:

Delisa Frontera 3rd EMG Chapter 15 (about 42 pages) *Table on page 355

Liveson, Jay. Peripheral Neurology: Case Studies. Third Edition. New York: Oxford University Press Inc., 2000. Print.

Preston DC, Shapiro BE.  Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders, 2nd Edition.  Boston: Butterworth-Heineman, 2005. Print.

Visco, Christopher J, Gary P Chimes, and James P McLean. Mclean Course In Electrodiagnostic Medicine. New York: Demos Medical, 2010.

Weiss, Lyn D, J K. Silver, and Jay Weiss. Easy Emg: A Guide to Performing Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography. Edinburgh: Butterworth-Heinemann, 2004. Paperback.

Suggested Reading from American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine (AANEM):  http://www.aanem.org/Education/Resources/References/Suggested-Reading.aspx

Written by a PGY-4 who just completed the rotation.

Getting access set up

Creating your CPRS electronic signature code

Your signature code is separate from your PIV PIN and is created in VistA. Set it up early and keep it private (never put it in a template).

  • Open VistA (Gold Star or VA Shortcuts). At the Main Menu enter TB (Toolbox), then ELE.

    Check your initials, signature block name and title (all in CAPS) and your VA office phone (not your cell). If REPLACE appears when editing your title, enter "...", press Enter, and retype the title in CAPS at WITH.

    Create the code: 6–20 letters or numbers, all uppercase, no Ctrl characters. Typing does not show on screen. Re-enter it to verify, then press Enter until you leave the Toolbox.

    If you skip the prompt or mistype the confirmation, go back to the Main Menu and repeat.

The EMG workflow

Start the machine: Turn on the monitor and the Cadwell (switch on the back left). Open Sierra and log in with username admin and password admin (press Enter if another prompt appears). For a new patient enter first name, last name and last four SSN digits as the ID. Click Start and pick a template (Bruno Upper Extremity, Bruno Lower Extremity, Cuevas).

Open the patient in CPRS: Clinic → search WPB Rehab EMG → choose the numbered clinic → choose the patient. "Save Clinic for Current Day" saves repeating the search. Useful tabs: Cover Sheet (PMH, meds, BMI); Reports → Local Imaging; Labs (A1c etc.); Consults (the EMG referral).

Review the consult: Open the most recent EMG referral; note the referring provider, reason, history and any attending recommendations. Decide which nerves to test before you start (attendings have different preferences).

Save note templates: Open a chart, create a temporary note, click Templates (lower left) → right-click → Create/Edit Template → name it, paste the text, Apply. Discard the temporary note. Shared templates: Shared Template → Physical Medicine → PM&R Physicians → EDx. Update the resident names in the signature section.

Start the note from the consult: Action → Consult Results → Complete/Update Results, so the note stays linked to the consult; pick the EMG note and the attending as co-signer. If Consult Results is grayed out, ask IT for: PAIN PROCEDURE OUTPATIENT; PHYSICAL MED & REHAB (EMG/NCS) OUTPATIENT; REHAB MD OUTPATIENT (the same permissions as your co-resident).

Write the note: Copy the referring provider and exact consult reason from the EMG order (use Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V). Update age, sex, handedness and a focused history (onset and progression, diabetes, thyroid disease, alcohol, prior treatment, prior EMG/NCS). Find prior VA study numbers for comparison. Use "Save Without Signature" for unfinished notes.

Results: Line up decimal points under the correct L/R columns. Wording: latency "prolonged", amplitude "low", conduction velocity "slow/slowed"; match singular/plural to the number of nerves or muscles. Interpret each nerve as you finish it and mark it with an asterisk.

Sign: Choose the correct attending as co-signer. Do not make yourself the primary provider (answer No or change it to the attending). Sign with your CPRS signature code.

Cadwell / Sierra tips

Control What it does
Scroll wheel Stimulus intensity
1 Distance entry (press 1, scroll to the cm value, press Store or 1)
2 Next nerve (arrange nerves in the order you will do them)
3 Averaging on/off (also the X-with-bar button on the Cadwell)
+/− Polarity (green probe light shows direction; for routine NCS point current toward the recording electrodes; F-waves and H-reflexes are exceptions)
Store Saves the selected waveform (it turns from white to purple)

  • Switching nerves resets intensity and polarity. Wipe gel off the probe between patients (alcohol swabs work well).

    Drag nerves to reorder the list; moving finished nerves to the top keeps them separate.

    To delete saved waveforms, Ctrl-click the purple ones, press Delete and confirm, then press F5 (Sort Traces) to reorder by latency.

    To reuse an earlier trace, click the multiple-waveform icon next to the star (upper right), select one trace (it turns yellow) and replace. Selecting two averages them into a blue trace.

    Add a nerve: right-click the nerve list → Insert (or the star icon). Add a study: star icon → Studies. If laterality is wrong, right-click the nerve and swap sides; no need to repeat the study.

    End of day: turn off the Cadwell (back left switch) and the monitor. Do not shut down the computer.

General Outpatient Rotation

Dress Code: Scrubs

Need: Laptop, Reflex Hammer

EMR System: (WRS) http://www.waitingroomsolutions.com/

Rotation Responsibilities and Protocols

By following these procedures, you ensure a smooth and efficient start to your day, helping to maintain a high standard of patient care and team communication.

  • Morning Commute:

    • Leave Early: Be sure to leave early, as traffic on Oakland Avenue can be unpredictable and often hectic. Allow extra time in the morning to ensure timely arrival at the office.

    Upon Arrival:

    • Log-in Procedure: Once you arrive, log in to the WRS (Workplace Reporting System).

      Patient Status: Patient names displayed in blue indicate that they have arrived and are waiting in a room to be seen.

      Room Assignment: Speak with the senior resident to confirm the room number of the waiting patients.

    Uniform Afternoon Stay: All residents are required to remain on duty until the afternoon. Early departures are not permitted unless explicitly approved by the attending physician.

    Dismissal Protocol: Senior residents are not authorized to dismiss medical students or junior residents. Only attending physicians have the authority to grant dismissal at the end of the workday.

    Medical Student Responsibilities:

    • Non-Procedural Role: Medical students are not licensed to perform procedures independently. Their primary responsibilities include taking notes, conducting patient intakes and interviews, and observing procedures performed by residents.

      Liability Awareness: Given that medical students are not insured to perform procedures, it is critical to adhere to this protocol to avoid liability issues (NO NEEDLE STICKS!!!).

      Inpatient rotation: if rotators are requesting inpatient experience they will require a level 2 background check with fingerprinting to be initiated at least 2 weeks prior to the hospital start date, and informing the attending (either Dr. Neubert or Dr. Vivaldi) of the medical student’s available dates.

      Medical students are here to learn and as such, having them complete notes should not supersede their educational needs. As a general rule, each resident on service should be writing more notes than any medical student rotating in the clinic each day. This is in addition to and not including patient visits that the resident may supervise the medical student for. Residents are still responsible for seeing their own patients and writing their own notes. Reports of residents not pulling their weight in the clinic will be handled as a lack of professionalism.

    Educational Opportunities:

    • Informal Presentations: Senior residents should allocate time for junior residents and medical students to conduct mini informal presentations 2-3 times per week.

By adhering to these guidelines, we ensure the safety of our patients, the legal compliance of our practices, and the educational enrichment of our medical team.

Established Patients: You will (for most patients) begin each patient with Electric Stimulation machines and heating pads. Have a senior resident show you how to use the E-stim if you are unfamiliar. After that, you go in, and talk to patients about current HPI, work on them with osteopathic manipulation (use common sense with elderly or injured), find out how the medications (if any) are controlling their pain levels, constipation, side effects, etc. Present to Dr. Diaz when he’s available, see the patient with him after you present. Some will request routine trigger point injections or joint injections. If you are unfamiliar, this is a great rotation to practice, you will do them daily. You also will be learning and using acupuncture techniques, ultrasound, and fluoroscopy occasionally. Become familiar with how to use this equipment early in your rotation so you won’t waste time learning it when you get to use it. When you are done seeing the patient, you will be responsible for cleaning your patient room (that involves taking the bed sheets each time, putting them in the laundry room, and replacing each room with clean sheets. Unplug any cords to any devices that patients could potentially trip over).

New Patients: With new patients, perform a complete H&P, formulate a list of differential diagnosis/workup/treatment plan in your head, and then present to Dr. Diaz. He will guide you through the encounter, and you will learn a lot about patient care with new patients in this office.

Notes: You will write your notes immediately after your patient encounter. If you do not finish your note before the next patient arrives, be sure you write down any procedures you performed, or any specialized equipment used (such as Ultrasound) as this will be important when you code for billing at the end of the note. *Please be aware that if a patient has Medicare B insurance, then you will NOT list certain procedures (such as E-stim, modalities, etc..) because Medicare does not reimburse for it, so you do not want to bill for it.

It is our responsibility to code and “marry” diagnosis with code.

99214: EVERY established patient

99204: EVERY new patient

G0283: E-stim

9892..: for OMT depending on the # of body regions, aim for 7-8 or 9-10

Body regions referred to are: head region; cervical region; thoracic region; lumbar region; sacral region; pelvic region; lower extremities, upper extremities; rib cage region; abdomen and viscera region.

Injections: Use tabs to code for trigger point or joint injection, also code for what medication is used under the “medication” tab.

98711 or 98713: Acupuncture +/- stim

*INCOMPLETE NOTES or MISSING CODING MAY RESULT IN FAILURE OF ROTATION*

Tips:

  • Office Procedures: On your first day, make sure to have a thorough orientation with the office manager to understand how things operate. This will help you integrate into the workflow smoothly.

    Respect Dr. Diaz's Time: Dr. Diaz is busy, so try to solve minor issues or questions yourself before bringing them to him. This shows respect for his time and demonstrates your independence in problem-solving.

    Self-Sufficiency: Bring snacks and drinks to sustain yourself during busy periods. Finding a moment to snack can help keep your energy levels up until you can take a proper break.

    Ultrasound Machine Usage: Follow the protocol for using the ultrasound machine diligently. Always keep it plugged in during use and storage to avoid data loss. Familiarize yourself with its functions early on so you're prepared to use it efficiently.

    Cell Phone Usage: Avoid using your cell phone for personal matters during work hours. Save it for lunch breaks to maintain professionalism and focus on your duties.

    Punctuality: Notify the office if you're going to be late, and inform your co-residents promptly. Punctuality is crucial in maintaining the efficiency of the workplace.

    Patient Safety: Always review a patient's medical history before any procedures, especially injections. This is crucial for handling situations like accidental needle sticks with patients who have infectious conditions.

    Proper Disposal and Protection: Dispose of needles in sharps containers and wear gloves during procedures to ensure safety. Additionally, wear a lead apron in the fluoroscopy lounge to minimize radiation exposure.

General Information:

In general, outgoing residents will get in contact with HR and get the onboarding and credentialing going for incoming residents. It’s fairly straightforward since they only need to activate your account from St. Catherine’s. However if needed: get in touch with Ana Martinez at least 2 weeks prior to starting your rotation so you can fill out the required paperwork. As with all rotations make sure you have your updated PPD, yearly flu shot, current ACLS/BLS Certification. I recommend having your own personal copies of medical records so if a rotation site ever needs it you can send it quickly.

Make arrangements to spend an hour or two with prior residents for adequate sign out and rundown of workflow.

Responsibilities:

Dr. Queiroz (“Dr. Q”) is a former Larkin Chief resident who works with you to escalate your responsibilities and to be a fairly independent inpatient rehab resident by the end of the rotation. He will show you how team conferences are held at the beginning of the rotation, and by the end of the first month you should be able to lead a team conference on your own. Due to Dr. Q’s busy schedule as an inpatient physician in several other locations including Encompass, several MedSpas and another location in Orlando, his rounding time is quite variable but he still generally both residents to be present for most rounds and splitting the census (regardless of how low it can be at times), except for times when he notifies you in advance that he cannot physically round himself which may require you to coordinate with his APRN instead. Communicate with the previous resident regarding his most recent rounding schedule, but in general expect to arrive around 8 AM. You will receive a vital log every morning. Make sure all patients are stable then take new admissions and finally see your follow-ups. Admission notes must be completed within 24 hours of the patient being admitted so do these first. Progress notes are to be completed the day you see the patient. Notes are written on the CHS EMR WellSky, and labs are available every Tuesday on ECS. Orders are placed on ECS as well, similarly to St. Catherine’s. Team conferences are held at 10am on Tuesday for every patient, and at 10am on Thursday for every patient admitted since Tuesday of that week (patients admitted overnight onto Thursday will likely be postponed until the following Tuesday team rounds). On rare occasions, team conferences can be held earlier at 9AM, but this will be communicated and it is usually at Dr Q’s discretion. In general, the secretary and nursing staff would appreciate it if you verbally inform them of any STAT orders you place, any labs or consults you order, and any discharge medication reconciliation printouts which are performed for all patients (except those going to SNFs) upon discharge. The rotation is overall quite similar to St. Catherine’s West from the PGY-2 year.

Catholic Health Services is a great organization to rotate with and a core part of our residency program. Be respectful to others as you work as part of an interdisciplinary team that is critical to patient care.

Parking: free, gate with guard will open automatically once you show guard your ID

Team conference days Tuesdays/Thursdays 10am

ST. ANTHONY'S PGY-3/4 GUIDE: A DAY IN THE LIFE

Written by residents for residents.

Census: 22 rooms (201–222); some rooms have more than one bed. The 2 PGY-3/4 residents split the census.

Hours: Dr. Q wants a resident in the hospital from 8 AM to 12 PM every day. Both residents do not need to be there the whole time; you can split shifts (for example 8–10 and 10–12). Be responsible and plan it with your co-resident.

Rounding: Dr. Q comes at different times, sometimes 6 AM on his own (he does not expect you then). For new patients he usually comes between 8 and 12 and asks the resident to present.

Team conference: 10 AM, usually in the big conference room (sometimes the small one; ask the nurses). If you are on the 10–12 shift, come early on team days and be prepared.

⚠ Confirm: this guide reports team conference on Monday and Friday (plus Thursday if needed for Monday/Tuesday-night admits); the section above says Tuesday/Thursday. Check with Dr. Q or Kristina (PPS coordinator) and update both.

Systems: Same ECS and WellSky as St. Catherine's. Check WellSky the night before for new admissions so you can split them, or call the floor and ask the night nurses. WellSky does not work well on iPhone browsers.

St. Anthony's vs St. Catherine's

  • Patients are mostly English-speaking, with some Creole speakers; many nurses speak Creole and can help translate.

    Smaller overall patient load.

    Dr. Q gives you much more independence to order what you think is best (within reason and what is available). You do not need to run everything by him, as long as you keep him informed.

    No one double-checks your orders the way Drs. Feliz and Neubert did, so be diligent. The nurses will often catch duplicate or wrong-chart orders.

Controlled substances

  • Place the order in ECS and write a prescription on the prescription pad (in the bin behind the nursing station), usually 30 tablets, and tell the nurses.

    At discharge, controlled substances cannot go through ECS. Write them on the pad for a 3-day supply and leave them for Dr. Q to sign (unless you have your own DEA number).

    Write the script at least the day before discharge so Dr. Q can sign it in the morning. For weekend discharges, have it written by Friday.

Discharge medication reconciliation (ECS)

  • Go to "View/Edit Current Orders" and click every medication the patient is going home on (the text turns red). Double-check the selection.

    Right-click and choose "Append All", then click the blue "Print Rx Providers Only" box. Wait until the screen closes on its own.

    On the main ECS screen, click the blue "Print Rx" box (bottom right), choose the patient and today, and print to the SJW printer.

    Write your NPI at the top of the first page, then enter the quantity with units on each script and sign it. Refills are 0; usually a 30-day supply. Check your math, because outside pharmacies will call if it does not make sense.

    Give discharge med-rec printouts for every patient except those going to a SNF.

Leading team conference

Dr. Q will show you how the first few times; aim to lead it on your own by the end of month 1. Report medical barriers to discharge, IV antibiotic timing, status changes and important labs. For a patient's first conference, give a one-liner or the diagnosis so everyone is on the same page. Stay engaged; therapists and Dr. Q may ask you questions.

Consultants and resources

  • Neuro: Wilson. Cardiology: Urbandt (NP Stephanie). Nephrology: Rosario (NP Anna; NP Rose). Pulm: Liebermann / Chaudhry. Psych: Carlos (Balanced Wellbeing). Palliative: Bloom Palliative (tell case management). ID: Chaudhari (NPs Shobha / Faisal alternate weeks).

    Ask Dr. Q which IM physician he wants. Patients from Westside usually have Sardinas (NP Greg). NP Rock works with Dr. Golalwala and Dr. Mendez.

    There is no lab or MDops login: check labs in ECS. Consultant notes are printed and placed in the chart.

    Radiology reports: the nurses print them and you sign to acknowledge you read them. Radiology site: pmdxu.com (User: SAhospital, Password: Pass1!).

    Gladys is the nurse for admissions. Her contact is (305) 297-3016. At 5-5:30PM you will receive a print out of projected admissions. This census will also be emailed to you if you have given your email to Yuri. The admission email will include the Pre-admission screening.

    Must stay until 10 PM. Cannot leave premises when you are on call. It is your responsibility to be available to the nursing staff so you can answer their questions, evaluate patients they are concerned about and run rapid response &/or codes. In the event of an emergency, you must notify Dr. Vivaldi if for any reason you need to leave early.

    Call your attending with any issues that are beyond your current level of expertise.

EPIC:

For those who don’t want to log in to a computer to place orders, here are the instructions to get Epic on your phone. Whole process takes maybe 15 minutes

1. Download Haiku app

2. Call the EPIC help desk (888) 972-1199

3. Tell them you want to get Haiku on your phone, they will ask for some information

4. Send the info to this email: smishaikurequests@selectmedical.com - They will send a link back to your email along with a PDF for user instructions.

5. Open the link on your phone, it will route to Haiku.

6. Login once Haiku opens and you’re golden 😊

PTO

  • You cannot take more than 5 days off in 3 months during this rotation (CME & Sick Days are not included)

Expectations

  • The night before, you should know who you are following and split up the census with your team with all projected admissions. New admissions should be divided accordingly (full hospital census will wax and wane, but you will carry between 12-14 patients on average).

    Pre-round time varies per attending, generally arrive at 6:30-7AM.

    New admissions have priority over established patients. Full H&P’s must be completed within 24 hours of new patient admission. This is VERY important. Check the time they arrived in the EMR.

    PGY2 residents work with Dr. Mamsaang and Dr. Vivaldi. PGY3 residents work with Dr. Ortiz and Dr. Ramirez. If one service gets more than 3 admissions per resident (6 per team), the other residents will help out with the admit and then pass the patient off to the service that will follow the patient.

    Your first physical exam must be your most thorough physical exam.

    Check heels and sacrum on every patient, and document your findings. It is better to document “Minimal/moderate sacral erythema appreciated”, than to document, “No sacral skin breakdown.” Make sure the patient’s nurse is aware of your findings.

    All progress notes should be completed by the end of your work day. Every progress note should include functional status, DVT prophylaxis, GI prophylaxis, and disposition.

    Internal Medicine is the primary team, so PM&R residents do not write discharge summaries. A progress note is still required on the day of discharge.

    You must be present at every rapid response. If a rapid response is announced, stop what you are doing immediately and go see the patient (unless you are in the middle of a procedure, of course.) PGY-2 residents are encouraged to run every rapid response.

    If a patient is acutely sent to the hospital please attempt to get a hold of the IM and consulted physicians for recommendations and orders. Call your attending.

    All residents are expected to remain present throughout the duration of team conference.

    Cafeteria provides complimentary meals for physicians. Do not abuse this courtesy. Please take a reasonable amount of food and supplement with your own food from home. Hours are breakfast 7-9AM and Lunch 11AM-2PM. If you are on long call, you may request another portion at lunch to take for dinner.

Saturday and Sunday (Weekend call)

  • One resident is expected to be on-call every weekend. Call schedules should be organized at the start of each new block.

    Contact Niurka Pedrera the administrative secretary and ask her which Attending is on call the weekend you are on call in a timely manner. Reach out to the on call Attending in a timely manner and ask them which time they start rounds, if you are expected to see new consults. Each Attending has their own style. Ask your seniors for tips.

    You will be responsible for rounding on your patients, addressing any issues, and completing your notes. You will round with the attending on call that weekend.

    Call your attending with any issues that are beyond your current level of expertise.

Academics

  • Grand Rounds: Grand rounds are held on Tuesday the 2nd & 4th week of the month in the 1st floor dining room at 10 am. When making a schedule, decide which resident will be presenting for each respective grand rounds and topic. Let Dr. Vivaldi know in advance which resident and topic they will be presenting. Presentations are typically 30 mins long.

    Ask Dr. Vivaldi for the mini lecture with attendings schedule. It is your job to remind your Attendings of upcoming lectures, typically done during Friday at lunch time

    Reach out OT/PT/SLP for lunchtime lectures on Tuesdays

GENERAL INFORMATION:

Dress professionally, (scrubs are acceptable, recommend wearing a white coat) unless otherwise instructed. Try to put as much energy as you can into this rotation.  The attendings are great doctors, and great people, and they are happy to have us onboard.  Get to know the therapists, as they will be able to provide you with insight into your patient's progress.  Remember that we are guests here, so act accordingly.  Treat the facility, therapists, nurses, and patients with respect.

WRITING NOTES:

Proper SOAP note writing is a skill that should have been acquired in medical school.  As a specialist, your progress notes should be more focused than when you were a medical student.  Avoid extraneous information, as it defeats the purpose of a progress note.  Just focus on what has happened since the last time you saw your patient.  Subjective section should include patient's current complaint (weakness, pain, difficulty breathing, etc.)  When describing pain, address onset, severity, quality, consistency, location, duration, and radiation.  A short review of systems, at the end of your subjective section, is always a good idea.  It is good practice to ask every patient about chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, eating, sleeping, and participation in therapy.

Start the objective section with vital signs (Tmax is useful if you are following a fever.)  Try to examine at least 7 areas on each exam, and include at least 3 findings in each area.

After the objective section, comment on the patient's functional status. Mobility, transfers, and ambulation are traditionally followed from physical therapy notes.  ADLs are traditionally followed from occupational therapy notes.  Speech therapy progress should be reported, if you are following a dysarthric or dysphagic patient.

If you are following labs or imaging studies, make sure you make a note of the results.

Assessment will address your patient's primary diagnosis, which is contributing to their gait and ADL dysfunction.  Your plan should be numbered in order of priority.  Number 1 will always be Gait and ADL dysfunction.  Here you should address how they are progressing, any barriers to progress, and whether or not any c es in their therapy regimen should be made.  Number 2 will be the primary diagnosis contributing to their gait and ADL dysfunction.  For example; Left TKA – Stable.  Decreased pain reported today.  Progressing well with therapy.  Continue pain medication.  Continue PT/OT.  Continue DVT PPx.  Follow-up with ortho on x/y/zzzz.  Monitor surgical site daily for any signs of infection.  Dressing changes daily, and as needed.  Remove staples on x/y/zzzz.  Et Cetera.  Number 3, and on, will be other diagnoses that you are following (but not necessarily managing).   It is perfectly fine to say ‘further management as per internal medicine’ for diabetes or hypertension, for example.  Close out your plan with DVT prophylaxis, GI prophylaxis, and disposition. Disposition is something that you will have to discuss with case managers.  Each day you should ask yourself: “Why is this patient here?”  “When will this patient be ready for discharge?”  “Will this patient be safe to return home, or will they require transfer to a SNF or LTAC?”

ROUNDING:

Reach out to attendings for specific rounding times as they may change day by day. Be ready to round by 7:30 AM with Dr. Ramirez. Dr. Vivaldi tends to round late morning or early afternoon. Dr. Ortiz rounds late afternoon. Dr. Mamsaang rounds at about 10am.

Finish chart reviewing and pre-rounding on patients before the attendings are ready to round with you.

TEAM CONFERENCE:

Dr. Ortiz Team Conference on Mondays and Wednesday 10:30 AM.

Dr. Vivaldi has Team Conference on Thursday at noon.

Dr. Ramirez has team conference on Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 AM

Dr. Mamsaang conference is Tuesdays and Friday at 12pm.

When sitting in team conference, be sure to pay attention to the following: For nursing, focus on continence, skin breakdown, and meal consumption.  For physical therapy, focus on mobility, transfers, and ambulation.  For occupational therapy, focus on upper body dressing, lower body dressing, and transfers.  For speech therapy, focus on communication, expression, aphasia, dysphagia and recommended diet.  For neuropsych, focus on objective measures of mental functioning, concentration, attention, memory, MMSE, and psychology. The question you should be asking yourself is “How is this patient progressing?”  “What are this patient’s barriers to progress?”  “What will this patient’s ultimate disposition be?”  Team conference is as much for the patient, as it is for the team.

LARKIN SOUTH MIAMI CONSULT SERVICE - INSTRUCTIONS

  • Check for any TKA (Total Knee Arthroplasty) or THA (Total Hip Arthroplasty) cases (95% of orthopedic cases happen on Mondays and Wednesdays), also check for cases you think would benefit from rehabilitation

Steps:

  • Go to Larkin, 2nd floor.

    Take the facesheet, scan it using the Notes app, and send it to the ISS front desk, ISS medical assistant, and ISS office manager.

    Log in to Medhost. Choose "My Group List" and click on the desired patient.

    On the facesheet, write the vital signs. Then, click on "Notes -> H&P" and write down the PMH (Past Medical History).

    Click on "Ancillary Notes" and look for PT (Physical Therapy) notes (usually written by Nelson). Write the PLOF (Prior Level of Function), for example: "Modified Independent with Rolling Walker. Lives with family in a single-level home, 1 step to enter."

    Next, write the CLOF (Current Level of Function), for example: "5 feet with RW, Max A."

    Look at the case manager notes to see D/C (Discharge) planning.

    Go say hi to patients, perform physical exams, etc.

    Write notes. See instructions below

    Text Dr. Diaz (`); he will call you around 4 pm to discuss cases.

HOW TO WRITE NOTES

  • We have to do our notes in HMS Medhost and copy them into WRS (just copy the whole HMS Medhost note into the HPI section on WRS, add your name under disposition, couple diagnoses, and billing code. The billing codes that we use in WRS system: New consults: Hospital, 99222 and Follow-ups: Hospital, 99232)

    Ask Senior Resident for current WRS password

    HMS Tips:

PATIENT LIST/ADMINISTRATIVE

  • Send patient list with facesheet PDFs for new patients. You can download the face sheets from medhost. At the top of the medhost clinical view screen, it is the "dashing sheet of paper" icon between the printer icon & computer screen icon. I usually send it from my home PC when I did quick chart review/census printing.

    ***Send PATIENT LIST + FACESHEET to these contacts:

Subacute Care Rehab Consult Service

Before rotation, contact current residents on service to schedule ½ day observation and resident-to-resident patient sign out. PLEASE NOTE: this rotation is MERGED with the LCH South Consults rotation.
